noticias.titulo: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
noticias.resumen: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
noticias.texto:
Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
- Published
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo was less than a year old â an infant clinging to his mother â when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat â to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Ãric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
"He definitely feels lonely," he says.
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.
"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes â the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King â who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes â remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."
African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.
In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.
It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate â a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."
Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.
The bonds between gorillas â what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.
No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully â perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.
These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen â when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.
"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.
Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."
Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."
But while those phases â of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.
Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.
"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."
That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.
"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.
"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

noticias.titulo: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
noticias.resumen: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.
noticias.texto:
After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
- Published
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

noticias.titulo: Twenty Years of Al Jazeera English: The Counternarrative
noticias.resumen: Two decades of AJE: Shaping media, amplifying unheard voices and driving global conversations.
noticias.texto:
Featured Documentaries
Twenty Years of Al Jazeera English: The Counternarrative
Two decades of AJE: Shaping media, amplifying unheard voices and driving global conversations.
In November 2006, Al Jazeera English went live with an audacious mandate: to challenge the traditional hegemony of Western media conglomerates and structurally invert the global news flow by providing a localised, uncompromising perspective from the Global South to the English-speaking world. To mark its 20th anniversary, this documentary delivers a definitive, multilayered chronicle of AJE’s trajectory from a disruptive alternative to dominant Western news media to the globally consumed news source it is today. The film seamlessly pairs an outside-in investigative lens with ground-up human testimony and internal insights. The film reflects on AJE’s historic coverage of global conflicts, the climate crisis, genocide and more in a drastically changing media landscape, all while balancing difficult decisions regarding where to focus resources, battling stigma as state-funded media and weathering the targeting of the channel’s journalists and bureaus while trying to remain true to AJE’s core principles.

noticias.titulo: ‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters
noticias.resumen: SpaceX's Starship successfully returned to its launchpad after orbiting in space.
noticias.texto:
‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters
SpaceX’s Starship has successfully returned to its launchpad after orbiting in space.
On a cloudy Saturday afternoon in the southern US state of Texas, a pair of large metallic arms stretched out and caught a giant in midair as it descended from the sky.
At 124 metres (407ft) tall, SpaceX’s Starship is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for travel to the Moon and Mars. Yet 22 hours after its latest blast off into space, it made history on Earth while returning, as it slipped smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase city in Texas.
Aerospace engineers across the globe have lauded the first-ever capture of the upper stage of a spaceship and welcomed the achievement, which signals that mega rockets could soon be fully reusable.
Here’s why the historic capture matters:
How did it work?
On Saturday, after orbiting Earth 14 times for 22.5 hours, SpaceX’s Starship emerged from thick clouds over its Starbase launch site, flipped itself to a vertical position and slowly descended into the arms on the ‘Mechazilla’ launch tower.
Like massive tweezers, the arms caught the upper stage of the spacecraft in midair, while its engines were still roaring.
The spacecraft then hooked onto the tower’s mechanical arms and shut off its engines.
The roaring sound was instantly replaced by loud cheers from watchers nearby – they had just seen for the first time in history the capture of a mega rocket.
“That was the missing link, the holy grail of spaceflight,” said SpaceX mission commentator Dan Huot. “We caught a Starship and now everything changes.”
“Congratulations to an incredible team at SpaceX!!!” SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said.
NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land astronauts on the Moon later this decade, also welcomed the achievement.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.
“Making more believers by the day…one step closer to [the moon],” he added.
Why was the capture tricky?
Spacecraft returning to Earth battle gravity and a range of atmospheric factors that are nearly impossible to perfectly predict or game.
Sputnik 1, the first-ever artificial satellite sent into space, burned up while returning to Earth.
Several manned spacecraft have been destroyed while re-entering the atmosphere, killing the astronauts on board.
In April 1967, the Soviet Union’s Soyuz 1 spacecraft re-entered the atmosphere successfully, but its parachutes failed to deploy properly. Cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died in the crash-landing near the Ural mountains. Decades later, NASA’s space shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry from orbit, killing all seven astronauts on board.
In recent decades, space agencies and private firms have made major advances in safety. But many spacecraft are impossible to reuse after splashing down in the sea or on land.
Since October 2024, SpaceX has on three occasions successfully caught the boosters that propel shuttles, once they have run out of fuel and separated from the main rocket.
But until now, the main spacecraft has never been successfully caught in midair.
Soon after its return, Musk and his engineers inspected the spaceship and said that everything appeared to have worked well, including its vital heat shield.
“Ship 42 looks great!” Musk wrote on X, posting photos and videos from the launch tower.
While the capture was tricky, aerospace engineers said the upper stage catch is a big success for SpaceX.
Niharika Patel, Technical Programme Manager at Loft Orbital, a US-based space infrastructure company, told Al Jazeera that watching the catch happen was “magical.”
“Landing a rocket back on Earth is incredibly difficult and can itself be considered an engineering marvel. Now add the sheer size and weight of Starship to that equation,” she said, noting that this is also the first time the upper stage booster has been successfully caught.
“It requires incredible precision to ensure the vehicle reaches exactly the right position, withstands the extreme heat of atmospheric re-entry and executes highly controlled manoeuvres within a very tight window. And all of this happens without a pilot — it’s completely autonomous,” she added.
Why does it matter for space technology advances?
SpaceX has become dominant in the aerospace industry primarily because the company has been trying to slash the cost of space travel by launching reusable rocket technology and rapid, repeat engineering.
So far, its Falcon 9 rocket has launched 700 times since 2010, with its first stage being reusable and its second stage discarded into the sea.
With Starship, Musk has said he wants to create fully reusable flights that can also transport humans into space with minimum refurbishment.
“SpaceX has already significantly reduced the cost of getting to orbit through Falcon 9’s reusability. It’s super cheap and convenient to send satellites to low Earth orbit. Starship takes this a step further by being a much bigger craft and aiming for full reusability of both the booster and the upper stage,” Patel said.
She explained that a fully reusable vehicle can be rapidly refurbished and flown again, dramatically increasing frequency and reducing cost. So if Starship reaches this milestone, Patel said it would make access to space even more affordable and scalable, just as commercial aviation transformed travel by making aircraft reusable with quick turnaround times between flights.
“This is essential for the next era of space exploration, from deploying large satellite constellations and building space infrastructure to enabling sustained human exploration of the Moon and Mars,” Patel added.

noticias.titulo: Can Netanyahu and Eisenkot form a ‘unity’ government in Israel?
noticias.resumen: Yashar and Likud are scheduled to hold talks on Sunday, but will need to overcome major differences to work together.
noticias.texto:
Can Netanyahu and Eisenkot form a ‘unity’ government in Israel?
Likud and Yashar, their parties, are scheduled to hold talks on Sunday, but will need to overcome major differences to work together.
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his appeal for a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, casting a coalition that would keep him in power as integral to Israel’s national security.
In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said his meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”. He said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all” and claimed Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.
Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party and the man given the first shot to form Israel’s next government by President Isaac Herzog, called Netanyahu’s appeal a “bluff”.
“Nice try, but these tricks don’t work on me. Nor on Israel’s citizens,” Eisenkot said.
But Eisenkot confirmed that Yashar and Netanyahu’s Likud Party were talking about the proposal for a shared government.
So what, if anything, would it take for them to govern together, and what other options does Eisenkot have?
How do the numbers in the Knesset add up?
In Israel’s October 27 election, the four-party bloc led by Eisenkot won 48 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53. Two Palestinian-led factions, the Joint List and Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List, won a record 19 seats between them.
Last week, Eisenkot’s bloc showed what it could do with the backing of both Palestinian-led factions, securing a 63-to-50 vote to approve the makeup of the Arrangements Committee, a panel that helps set the Knesset’s agenda while coalition talks are under way. The bloc then moved to set up temporary committees overseeing finance, foreign affairs and defence.
Eisenkot’s bloc and the two Arab-led factions hold 67 seats combined, six more than needed for an outright majority. Another possibility is a minority government backed by Ra’am’s eight lawmakers. Their support would give Eisenkot 56 votes against Netanyahu’s 53 if the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers abstained or stayed away from the confidence vote. That would allow a government to take office with fewer than 61 votes in favour, but it would depend on how all three groups voted.
But getting Eisenkot’s allies to agree to such a deal is another matter. Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats, is open to working with the Palestinian-led factions, while Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman and Together leader Naftali Bennett have rejected a coalition with Palestinians. However, both served in the government formed in 2021, when Ra’am became the first Arab party to formally join an Israeli governing coalition.
“One of Eisenkot’s main difficulties is the opposition of Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett [leaders of parties in his alliance] to relying on Arab parties,” Yasser Manna, a researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Studies on Israeli Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “This position restricts Eisenkot’s coalition options, but it does not automatically make a unity government with Netanyahu more likely. Instead, it increases the importance of negotiations with other parties, particularly the ultra-Orthodox parties.”
The other main option, which according to experts is the most likely scenario, is the Eisenkot bloc going into a coalition with both ultra-Orthodox parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which would take the Eisenkot bloc to 61.
Advisers from one faction of United Torah Judaism have reportedly sought a written commitment from all 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot’s bloc to pass a law exempting Jewish religious seminary students from military service and to shield it from being struck down by the High Court. Eisenkot and Lieberman are reportedly opposed to this compromise.
Could Eisenkot and Netanyahu govern together?
President Herzog gave Eisenkot until December 6 to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days, which would take the deadline to December 20.
Eisenkot has left the door open to members of Netanyahu’s Likud Party and to far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, provided they back a government led by Eisenkot and accept his programme.
“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said at the ceremony where Herzog handed him the mandate.
Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that agreeing to meet can serve both men politically. “The coalition formation period is about spin and distortion and trying to gain leverage,” he told Al Jazeera. “So you take a meeting to show that you were willing to talk, then say the other side made unreasonable demands.”
The two men know each other well. Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and served as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet during the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. He left the emergency government in June 2024.
“I believe the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot is marked by a deep crisis of trust that goes beyond political competition,” Manna said. “However, it is important to distinguish between their political disagreements and their relatively similar approaches to national security. Both prioritise military and security considerations, particularly regarding the Palestinians and Iran.”
An early test could come on Tuesday, when Eisenkot’s allies plan to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud with Yashar lawmaker Matan Kahana. Eisenkot has challenged Netanyahu and Smotrich to back Kahana and allow the vote to go ahead as scheduled, saying their response would show how serious they are about cooperation.
But even if Eisenkot and Netanyahu agreed on a policy plan for government, they still have to decide who leads. “The question of who would serve as prime minister remains the central obstacle,” Manna said. “Eisenkot has so far rejected a rotation arrangement with Netanyahu.”
Could a security crisis change the talks?
Meanwhile, Netanyahu is still in office as caretaker prime minister while negotiations continue. That gives him an incentive to exploit divisions among Eisenkot’s potential partners and wait for his mandate to run out, experts say.
“At this stage, Netanyahu does not necessarily need to form a new coalition himself,” Manna said. “Preventing Eisenkot from forming one may be enough to preserve his position temporarily.”
Manna said Netanyahu could also use a security crisis to increase pressure for a national government. “A renewed large-scale confrontation could increase pressure for a national unity government or shift the priorities of coalition negotiations,” he said. “At the same time, it could generate new disagreements over military decision-making, the management of the conflict, and the authority of a caretaker government.”
If talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties fail, Levy said, Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between accepting support from the Palestinian-led parties and leaving Netanyahu in office. He could also propose a short-lived government whose immediate purpose would be to replace Netanyahu and prepare for another election.
He added that in such a scenario, Eisenkot might tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.
This would prevent Netanyahu from using “his position as prime minister to create a crisis”.

noticias.titulo: Germany vs Netherlands: Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
noticias.resumen: Germany will likely need to win on Monday to reach the quarterfinals unless Serbia beat Greece away from home.
noticias.texto:
Germany vs Netherlands: Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
Germany will likely need to win on Monday to reach the quarterfinals unless Serbia beat Greece away from home.
Who: Germany vs Netherlands
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A2
Where: Olympiastadion in Berlin, Germany
When: Monday at 8:45pm (19:45 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.
Germany and the Netherlands head into the final Group A2 Nations League match hoping to secure their place in the quarterfinals.
Xavi Hernandez’s Netherlands side are practically through – barring a huge swing in goal difference – as they lead the table with 11 points after thrashing Greece 7-0 on Friday.
Jurgen Klopp’s Germany, who beat bottom placed Serbia 3-1 in their last game, know they will likely need a win to progress.
The Germans sit third with eight points, level with second-placed Greece but below them on their head-to-head record, which trumps goal difference as a tiebreaker in this season’s competition. Greece host Serbia, who have yet to win a point.
What happened in Germany’s last game?
Germany cruised to a 3-1 win against Serbia in Belgrade on Friday.
The Germans forced Serbia’s Srdan Babic into an early own goal with Florian Wirtz and Brajan Gruda also scoring.
Babic made up for his blunder with a second-half consolation strike while Serbia finished with nine men after substitutes Vanja Dragojevic and Andrija Zivkovic were sent off late on.
Germany have now won twice, drawn twice and lost once in five games under Klopp.
What happened in the last Netherlands game?
Tijjani Reijnders netted a first-half hat-trick as the Netherlands thrashed Greece 7-0.
The Dutch were 5-0 up at the break with Crysencio Summerville putting the hosts ahead in the sixth minute before Reijnders ran riot and Jurrien Timber notched their fifth before half-time.
Timber scored again just before the hour mark with Donyell Malen netting the final goal.
Germany looking forward to ‘final’ against Netherlands, Klopp says
Klopp says his side are happy to have set up a deciding match against the Dutch.
“We wanted to set up a final against the Netherlands in Berlin, and now we have it,” Klopp said.
“We now have the chance to secure qualification for the next round in our own hands. We want to show everyone that German football is in good hands,” he said.
“We have good players, we’re working hard and we want to show in these matches that we’ve learned, that we’ve come together and that we’ve developed as a team. And that was definitely evident [against Serbia].
“The atmosphere in the camp is good, but that brings nothing if nobody can see it on the pitch. Our first job is to show the world that we can play football.”
Predictions
The Opta supercomputer has made Germany the favourites with a win probability of 43.5 percent.
The Netherlands were given a 29.8 percent chance of winning while a draw was estimated at a 26.8 percent likelihood.
Head-to-head
- Previous matches: 49
- German wins: 18
- Draws: 19
- Dutch wins: 12
What happened in their last encounter?
Cody Gakpo volleyed in a stoppage-time equaliser to rescue a 1-1 draw for the Netherlands against Germany in their Nations League Group A2 opener on September 24, denying Klopp a winning start to his tenure.
The visitors took a first-half lead with Felix Nmecha slotting in from close range. Karim Adeyemi should have scored another, but he somehow missed the target from 5 metres (5.5 yards) out.
The Dutch upped the pressure after the break and repeatedly came close to an equaliser with Germany’s new number one goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen making several good saves. But their dominance finally paid off with Gakpo’s late strike.
Germany’s team news
Bayern Munich stars Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry are unavailable due to muscle problems, but Germany have no other reported injury concerns.
Predicted starting XI:
Ter Stegen (goalkeeper); Treu, Thiaw, Tah, Mittelstadt; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz
Netherlands team news
Frenkie de Jong has returned to Barcelona for treatment after he went off with a back injury during the win over Greece. Teun Koopmeiners looks set to replace him in midfield.
Captain Virgil van Dijk did not join the squad during this international break due to injury, so Tottenham duo Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke are likely to start as centre backs.
Predicted starting XI:
Verbruggen (goalkeeper); Dumfries, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Timber; Veerman, Koopmeiners; Summerville, Reijnders, Gakpo; Malen

noticias.titulo: Gaza families bury bodies of loved ones trapped for years under rubble
noticias.resumen: The remains of 69 Palestinians have been recovered in northern Gaza, allowing families to bury them.
noticias.texto:
Gaza families bury bodies of loved ones trapped for years under rubble
The remains of 69 Palestinians have been recovered in northern Gaza, allowing families to finally bury relatives they had spent years searching for.
Jabalia, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Nabhan, a man in his sixties from Bir an-Naaja in northern Gaza, had waited more than three years for this day.
He wanted to give his loved ones a proper burial after 17 members of his family, including his seven children and grandchildren, were killed when their home was targeted 20 days after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Among those killed was Nabhan’s 45-day-old grandchild.
After years of searching for their bodies, on Sunday Nabhan was finally able to bury his family members after Civil Defence teams retrieved their remains from the rubble of his home.
“All of them were children, all of them were loved ones,” he said.
Nabhan said there had been no fighters, Israeli soldiers or captives inside the home when it was struck.
For the past three years, he had tried to help recover his family’s remains, but the difficult conditions prevented this.
Their recovery from his destroyed home brought some relief for Nabhan, but it also brought more trauma.
“It feels as if they have just been killed again. The wounds have reopened,” he said. “But, thank God, we now know that our children have a grave here, beside their siblings, and we can visit them.”
Waiting for a burial
The genocide in Gaza killed at least 73,600 people, with 82 per cent of the structures in Gaza damaged and two-thirds of them destroyed by waves of Israeli air strikes and shelling.
Under the rubble were thousands of bodies, with the continued attacks by Israeli forces often making it too dangerous for families or Civil Defence teams to retrieve them.
A truce agreed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, which has been repeatedly broken by Israel, has allowed for some of the bodies to be recovered from the rubble that carpets Gaza
Civil Defence teams have managed to retrieve the remains of 69 Palestinians from locations in Jabalia refugee camp and Beit Lahiya in recent days.
For many families, the operation marked the end of years of uncertainty. Relatives had repeatedly followed up with Civil Defence, waiting for heavy machinery and other equipment to reach bodies trapped under collapsed buildings.
Fatima al-Masri, 47, said her husband and 18-year-old son were killed in an Israeli attack in the Safatwi area of northern Gaza in October 2024. Their remains have been buried beneath the rubble of their home for two years.
“Every month, every two months, sometimes every week or every two weeks, we would follow up with Civil Defence,” she said. “They told us they needed heavy equipment to lift the house because several floors had collapsed on top of them.”
After a long delay, the recovery operation began, with workers digging through the rubble using machines and by hand. They found bone fragments and al-Masri’s son’s mobile phone, along with the bodies and belongings of those who had been with her husband and son.
“Thank God, we found their remains and everything that was with them,” al-Masri said.
The two years of tortuous delays had left her in a constant state of anxiety. Every day, the same questions occupied her thoughts.
“I was always tense and worried. Every day, the same question was in my mind: ‘When would they recover them? When would we be able to bring them out?’” she said.
After the remains were recovered, she expressed relief that her husband and son could finally be buried.
Thousands under the rubble
The Palestinian Civil Defence estimates that more than 8,000 bodies are still to be recovered across Gaza.
The total number of missing Palestinians is estimated to exceed 10,000, although the broader figure includes people whose whereabouts remain unknown for different reasons, including those believed to be buried under rubble, detained or buried without identification.
Israel’s ongoing siege on Gaza means that Civil Defence teams have limited resources, with manual excavation often the only way to do their grim work.
According to Palestinian authorities cited by the United Nations, more than 630 bodies and human remains had been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025 by September 2026.
Ramiz Hassouna, a lecturer at Israa University, said the recovery of his brother’s remains, Montaser, brought nearly two years of uncertainty to an end.
He disappeared on November 8, 2024, during the Israeli military siege of Jabalia refugee camp. He was last known to be in the al-Faluja area, where he had been trapped with a group of friends.
For almost two years, the family received conflicting accounts about his fate. Some said he had been killed, while others believed he had been detained.
The uncertainty ended when Civil Defence teams recovered his remains from a destroyed building in al-Faluja and contacted the family.
He was identified through personal belongings, including his wristwatch, a miswak (a traditional teeth-cleaning stick) and a prayer booklet, as well as distinctive marks on his front teeth.
Hassouna could not bring himself to go and identify his brother’s remains, so asked his younger brother to go in his place.
“I personally could not bear to look at my brother in that condition. I left it to my younger brother to identify him,” he said.
The remains of the friends Montaser was with when he died were recovered together and buried in the same grave.
“As they accompanied one another in this life, they will accompany one another in the afterlife,” said Hassouna.

noticias.titulo: Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
noticias.resumen: Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds, but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.
noticias.texto:
Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.
Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.
An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.
Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.
Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.
“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.
The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.
It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.
Tit-for-tat attacks
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.
Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.
Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.
US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.
However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.
“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Al Jazeera English marks 20 years: Stories that shaped the journey
noticias.resumen: Here are some of the crucial events Al Jazeera English has covered over the past two decades.
noticias.texto:
Al Jazeera English marks 20 years: Stories that shaped the journey
Here are some of the crucial events Al Jazeera English has covered over the past two decades.
Al Jazeera English is marking 20 years since its official launch on November 15, 2006, about 10 years after Al Jazeera Arabic was inaugurated.
Since then, the channel and its digital footprint have grown dramatically in terms of content and coverage, becoming one of the most influential outlets in the world with employees from 78 nationalities and 48 bureaus around the world.
Here are some of the most significant developments we have covered over the years:
Gaza war of 2008
The war went on for 22 days. Israel’s widespread aerial bombing campaign on densely populated areas of the Palestinian enclave, including homes, police stations, schools, United Nations buildings and hospitals, was followed by a ground assault.
About 1,400 Palestinians and 13 Israelis were killed in the war that led to a blockade being imposed on the Gaza Strip.
In the years that followed, attempts by activists to break that siege were met with a brutal response from Israel. The deadliest of those Israeli attacks was on the Mavi Marmara, a ship that was part of the Gaza Freedom Flotilla, a convoy carrying more than 700 activists and 10,000 tonnes of humanitarian aid. Israeli soldiers boarded the vessel early in the morning on May 31, 2010, firing at the civilian passengers. Ten Turkish nationals were killed, and the attack set off a major diplomatic spat between Israel and Turkiye.
Arab Spring
The series of pro-democracy and antigovernment protests, some of which led to armed rebellions after authorities brutally cracked down on them, started in December 2010 in Tunisia.
They swept across the Middle East and North Africa in the early 2010s, leading to multiple revolutions and shifts in power in Tunisia and Egypt, and prolonged conflicts in Syria, Libya and Yemen.
Many other countries introduced national reforms in light of the public movements going on across the region.
Taliban’s return to power
The Taliban movement returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 in line with an agreement between the armed group and the United States.
The administration of US President Donald Trump signed the deal with the Taliban in Doha, Qatar, in February 2020, which set a timeline for the complete withdrawal of US troops and allied armies from Afghanistan.
As US troops withdrew, the Taliban continued to take control of the country. In August 2021, Taliban fighters entered the capital, Kabul, unopposed after President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.
Russia’s war on Ukraine
In February 2022, the Russian army launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in a move widely perceived as unprovoked.
The attack, dubbed the “special military operation” by Moscow, resulted in widespread condemnation from the international community and started a brutal war, which is still ongoing.
Large chunks of eastern Ukraine – as well as the Crimean Peninsula, officially annexed by Moscow in 2014 – remain under Russian control today, with clashes and intense mutual aerial attacks on each other’s territory ongoing.
FIFA World Cup 2022
Qatar hosted the football World Cup in 2022, the first in the Middle East and Arab world. Due to summer heat in the Gulf, it was the first World Cup held in late autumn and winter.
Argentina won the championship, defeating France in the final.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza
Israel launched its genocide against Palestinians in Gaza on October 7, 2023, and it is ongoing even today despite a so-called “ceasefire” agreed in October 2025.
The inhumane war started after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 others captive.
Since then, the enclave has been almost destroyed, and more than 74,600 people have been killed, according to local authorities.
US-Israel war on Iran
The US and Israel launched strikes against Iran this February and started a war that killed many high-ranking Iranian officials, including the country’s supreme leader at the time, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Since then, the sides have exchanged attacks numerous times, with the US forces hitting Iranian territory and Tehran targeting what it says are US assets in the region.
The conflict led Iran to effectively block navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for hydrocarbon deliveries from the Gulf to the rest of the world, by attacking vessels passing through it.
The US, in response, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports aimed at crippling the country’s economy.
The process to reach a deal between the sides continues under the mediation of Qatar and Pakistan.

noticias.titulo: Kayla ⁠⁠Harrison defeats Amanda Nunes to retain UFC bantamweight belt
noticias.resumen: Harrison won by a fourth-round submission against MMA legend Nunes, who made a comeback after a three-year absence.
noticias.texto:
Kayla Harrison defeats Amanda Nunes to retain UFC bantamweight belt
Harrison won the fight by a fourth-round submission against MMA legend Nunes, who made a comeback after a three-year absence.
Kayla Harrison has retained her Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) bantamweight title with a fourth-round submission win over one of the mixed martial arts (MMA) all-time greats, Amanda Nunes, in the United States.
The American fighter leveraged her tremendous grappling skills and thwarted her opponent’s attempt to take the belt back in the main event of UFC 334 at New York’s Madison Square Garden on Saturday.
A two-time Olympic judo champion, the 36-year-old Harrison was facing arguably the greatest female fighter of all time in Nunes, a dominant two-weight champion at bantamweight and featherweight before she stepped away from the sport in June 2023. But the Brazilian could not shake off the rust from her long absence as she let the fight slip away from her.
Nunes did well initially, looking crisp in her striking and avoiding some early takedown attempts, but she eventually succumbed to Harrison’s grappling attack, spending much of the latter part of the opening two rounds on the bottom in a scarf-hold position from which she struggled to escape.
Emboldened by her success, Harrison displayed the full range of her judo skills with perfectly timed trips and tosses and vice-like ground control. In the fourth round, she chased Nunes down to the mat, jumping on her back and quickly sinking in a rear-naked choke that forced the 38-year-old to submit.
“I think I’m still in shock,” said Harrison, who had surgery on herniated disks in her neck in January.
“It feels surreal. Sometimes I can’t believe my life. I’m just really grateful, I’m humbled, it’s an honour and a privilege to stand before you,” she said, addressing her opponent.
Harrison (20 wins, one defeat) admitted she was not sure what was next for her but took a moment to acknowledge the audience.
“New York City, I love you,” she exclaimed after the fight.
Nunes (23 wins, six defeats) took her gloves off but did not make herself available for a post-fight interview.
Meanwhile, Ciryl Gane of France defeated American Josh Hokit by unanimous decision to retain the heavyweight title after a bruising five-round battle fought at a frenetic pace.
Gane successfully defended his title for the first time, sweeping the scorecards 48-47, 48-47, 48-47 against Hokit.
The first round saw Gane (15 wins, two defeats) get up quickly from an early takedown by Hokit (10 wins, one defeat), then land a few sharp jabs, uppercuts and an overhand right as he countered Hokit’s forward pressure. Hokit did, however, close the round with a slam with about 30 seconds remaining.
Hokit came back in the second round. After Gane stuffed an early single-leg attempt, Hokit pushed forward with determination, trading heavy right hands and clinching along the fence in a very physical exchange.
Hokit carried that momentum into the third round with a scramble takedown, then worked Gane over with several clinch elbows and foot stamps before flashing him the middle finger at the bell. As Hokit’s punches began to fade in the fourth round, Gane took control, countering the challenger’s fence clinches with several body kicks, knees to the midsection and short, dirty-boxing uppercuts.
With the result still in the balance in the fifth round, Gane stuffed Hokit’s takedown attempts and opened a cut just above his left eye, then dominated the striking with jabs, body shots and multi-punch combinations through the end of the round.
Gane kept things simple after the fight, as did the typically brash Hokit.
“It was an amazing fight,” Gane said.
Hokit said he would enjoy the moment, even if he was on the receiving end.
“Resilience builds character,” Hokit said.

noticias.titulo: Bahrain accuses Iran of attacking its territory to ‘settle’ score with US
noticias.resumen: Tehran says its air attacks on countries cooperating with the US are justified under international law.
noticias.texto:
Bahrain accuses Iran of attacking its territory to ‘settle’ score with US
Iran’s Foreign Ministry says its air attacks on countries cooperating with the US are justified under international law.
Bahrain’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denounced what it describes as “a resumption of Iran’s aggression” after the latest air attacks on its Riffa Air Base by Tehran.
In a statement, the ministry said the attacks on Sunday launched by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) violated international law and “no pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty”.
“Bahrain also rejects the use of its territory to settle accounts and holds Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences,” the statement added.
Bahrain’s military said its defence systems intercepted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom. Its Riffa Air Base is used by the United States military.
The IRGC has not commented. It had said on Friday that it launched an attack on a US early warning radar facility in Bahrain and destroyed it. Bahrain said it intercepted two drones that day.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, noted that Iran had held back amid intermittent US attacks in the past weeks but in the past three days, it has fired twice at Bahrain.
“We were seeing the United States’s low-intensity warfare being conducted against Iran. From time to time, the US attacked Iran’s military assets – telecommunications towers specifically – in the southern part of the country,” he said.
But that appears to have changed. “It seems this is now the new rule of engagement,” Serdar added.
Iranian minister says attacks justified
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Tehran’s attacks and accused Gulf countries of aiding US strikes against Iran.
“All the cases that indicate the role of the countries of the region in helping the US to attack Iran have been documented,” Baghaei said at a news conference on Sunday, adding that Tehran was taking diplomatic action and would “follow up on this issue seriously”.
He said missiles, drones and aircraft launched from military bases in neighbouring countries as well as logistical support provided to US forces were proof of these nations’ involvement.
“The responsibility of this group of countries in the region for the consequences … of the military aggression of the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran is clear,” Baghaei charged, referring to Israel.
Attacks on its neighbours, he said, were justified under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, which established the rights of states to defend themselves from attacks.
“No action has been taken by Iran against the sovereignty of these countries,” Baghaei said, arguing that Tehran’s attacks are “purely defensive in nature” and have targeted only US military bases and assets used to attack Iran.
Meanwhile, Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said in a post on X that it “condemned Iran’s brutal attacks on the sister kingdom of Bahrain as a flagrant violation of its sovereignty, a threat to its security, stability and territorial integrity”.
Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the country “reiterates its categorical rejection” of attacks threatening the region’s stability.
“The security of Bahrain and the Gulf states is closely linked to Egyptian national security and is one of the pillars of Arab national security,” the statement added.

noticias.titulo: Australia crush New Zealand to win fourth Women’s Rugby League World Cup
noticias.resumen: Australia dominated the first half and capitalised on the Kiwi Ferns’ errors to win 34-10 and clinch the trophy.
noticias.texto:
Australia crush New Zealand to win fourth Women’s Rugby League World Cup
Australia dominated the first half and capitalised on the Kiwi Ferns’ errors to win 34-10 and clinch the trophy.
Winger Jaime Chapman collected a hat-trick as Australia crushed New Zealand 34-10 on Sunday with an emphatic first-half performance to clinch their fourth consecutive Women’s Rugby League World Cup title.
Two tries in the opening five minutes did the damage, and there were four more before half-time to send the Jillaroos to the break with a commanding 34-6 advantage.
Despite applying pressure, they were unable to add to their score as the humid conditions in Brisbane took their toll and errors crept in.
But Australia had done enough to ensure a fourth straight title, beating the Kiwi Ferns in the final each time, to reinforce their status as the sport’s powerhouse nation.
“I want to thank the Kiwi Ferns. It’s been such a great rivalry for so many years now, with so much respect between the two of our teams,” said Australia captain Isabelle Kelly, now a three-time World Cup champion.
“To my team … I’m just so humbled and honoured to be able to lead you guys. This has definitely been a dream come true, and I knew that we could get the job done.”
Before Australia’s global rise, New Zealand won the World Cup in 2000, 2003 and 2008.
“We didn’t quite get the job done today, but we are going to assert dominance back into this jersey,” said New Zealand skipper Raecene McGregor.
“The best of the Kiwi Ferns is yet to be shown, so stay with us.”
New Zealand had won only one of their previous 12 Tests against the Jillaroos dating back to 2017, and they were under the pump immediately.
A knock-on near the New Zealand try line just two minutes in allowed Australia to spread the ball wide, and Chapman dived over in the corner for her 11th try of the tournament.
With all the momentum, Australia pressured New Zealand into another mistake and capitalised, with Shaylee Bent crashing over for their second converted try.
Midway through the first half, they were 18-0 ahead, with another Chapman special on the back of a lightning break.
A sensational solo effort from Jessica Sergis stretched the lead further, with the five-eighth shrugging off three tackles to sprint the length of the field.
New Zealand finally got on the board when Shannon Mato barged across, but Chapman’s third came after she burst through two tackles to race away, putting Australia back in full control before Tamika Upton added a sixth before half-time.
Australia started strongly in the second half with only some desperate Kiwi defence keeping them at bay.
But it was a much tighter affair, with New Zealand’s Mackenzie Wiki crossing in the dying seconds for the only try of the half.

noticias.titulo: Siege on Hebron’s Beit Ula industrial zone threatens Palestinian economy
noticias.resumen: Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in the occupied West Bank.
noticias.texto:
Siege on Hebron’s Beit Ula industrial zone threatens Palestinian economy
Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in the occupied West Bank.
Beit Ula, occupied West Bank – Fayez al-Amleh, 63, scans his factory in an industrial complex in this town northwest of Hebron and reflects on the recent Israeli measures that could cost him his business.
The production lines at TB.LOC, which produce security and fire-resistant doors, still slowly whir away. But they very nearly came to a halt when Israeli forces sealed the entrances to the Beit Ula industrial zone with earthen berms and stone barriers on November 4.
The measures have isolated roughly 60 Palestinian businesses from their customers and suppliers, which threatens the livelihoods of 2,500 workers employed in the industrial zone.
“Today, raw materials cannot get in, and we cannot get our products out of the industrial zone,” al-Amleh told Al Jazeera.
Hebron and the surrounding areas were hit hard by Israeli military operations after two Israeli soldiers were killed by suspected Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city on October 23.
Thousands of Palestinians were forced out of their homes during the 10-day siege on Hebron and returned only when Israeli soldiers left the city on November 2.
Siege on Hebron
The siege on Hebron, an economic hub for the occupied West Bank, led to losses of more than 12 million shekels ($3.8m) a day, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari.
But just days after the siege on Hebron was lifted, the blockade on Beit Ula’s industrial zone began. This has significantly impacted the operations of al-Amleh’s factory and the lives of the 70 workers his business employs.
As a result, his employees have had their hours cut or moved to part-time work, reducing their take-home pay.
Since the closure, daily sales for al-Amleh’s business have dropped from 70,000 shekels ($21,988) to between 2,000 and 3,000 shekels ($628 to $942).
Beit Ula has facilities that shape metal and make doors, electrical cabinets, sponge, cardboard and construction materials. Their activities are connected to a wider network of commercial and service businesses that depend on the continued movement of supplies and goods.
Agricultural activities on the surrounding land have also been affected along with suppliers and traders whose daily business depends on the factories.
Israeli forces have carried out a series of measures around the town of Beit Ula, including the demolition of four industrial facilities and the establishment of a nearby settlement outpost.
These measures are viewed by Palestinians in the area as part of a broader Israeli effort to take control of land surrounding the industrial zone and threaten economic and agricultural activity in the area.
Al-Amleh said that if the siege on the industrial zone continues more factories could be forced to shut down. This would severely impact the economic viability of Beit Ula and nearby towns, which rely heavily on the industrial zone for employment and secondary businesses.
He rejected an allegation by Israel that Beit Ula is responsible for the movement of workers into Israel without work permits, the reason Israel has given for imposing restrictions on the industrial zone. Instead, he considers it to be a form of collective punishment against Palestinian businesses and workers based there.
Ayman al-Adam, who has worked at the industrial zone for about three years, said the Israeli blockade on Beit Ula threatens the incomes that he and hundreds of other employees rely on to support their families.
“This road closure is not just a closure. It is closing the doors of livelihood for all the workers,” he told Al Jazeera.
‘Economic warfare’
The Israeli military and settlers have embarked on a campaign of disruption and intimidation against Palestinian businesses across the West Bank in recent months.
Settler pogroms have seen West Bank olive farmers routinely attacked during this year’s harvest and Palestinian crops, olive trees and livestock stolen.
An expansion of Israeli checkpoints across the West Bank has also restricted the movement of goods and people, hitting Palestinian businesses hard.
Palestinian Minister of National Economy Mohammad al-Amour said the Israeli measures targeting economic facilities in the West Bank amount to a war on the Palestinian economy.
“About 60 economic facilities along with their workers and all aspects of their production have been completely isolated from the Palestinian economy,” al-Amour told Al Jazeera. “This situation has become a burden on the Palestinian economy instead of being a source of support and contributing to it.”
Mahmoud Allan, head of the North Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, has appealed to authorities to halt the apparent Israeli campaign against Palestinian business.
“If this area is not reopened very quickly, some of the facilities that are major establishments in this licensed industrial zone in Beit Ula will be disrupted and forced to close,” he said.
“Factories can no longer operate normally. Workers have lost their income, and business owners are struggling to keep their businesses alive.”

noticias.titulo: Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas
noticias.resumen: Mansour Abbas faces mounting pressure from Israel’s change bloc to denounce Hamas as a prerequisite for coalition role.
noticias.texto:
Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas
Mansour Abbas faces mounting pressure from Israel’s change bloc to denounce Hamas as a prerequisite for coalition role.
The question of whether Mansour Abbas, the leader of Israel’s United Arab List (Ra’am), is willing to recognise the Palestinian group Hamas as a “terrorist” organisation may determine whether his party will play a role in the country’s next government.
According to Israel’s Ynet news website, Abbas has signalled to parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he would agree to the designation in exchange for a “genuine partnership” in a coalition led by Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming a new government after last month’s elections.
Eisenkot has made recognising Hamas as a “terrorist” group one of the conditions for joining his prospective coalition. He has also demanded that Abbas recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state – despite Abbas’s own identity as a Palestinian citizen of Israel.
But on Wednesday, Abbas denied that he had made a declaration on Hamas. Earlier in the week, he had simply reiterated Ra’am’s support for disarming Hamas, and condemning “terrorism”.
The demands concerning Hamas and recognising Israel as a Jewish state pose a problem for Abbas, whose party represents Palestinian citizens of Israel – around 20 percent of the population, excluding the millions who live under Israeli occupation in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
He wants to join the government – and has previously done so in the past, in 2021 – seeing it as a way to improve the lives of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and force Netanyahu and other far-right figures out of power.
But declaring Hamas a “terrorist” group would be seen by critics as tantamount to supporting the Israeli narrative, during a genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera that Eisenkot’s conditions are intended to make a partnership with Ra’am more acceptable to his Jewish Israeli supporters and coalition partners.
“Eisenkot is telling them practically that Ra’am’s votes will help him form the government, and that this partnership will take place according to the definition he wants for the state,” Jabareen said.
Including Ra’am’s eight seats in parliament would go a long way to helping Eisenkot secure a viable coalition. His own bloc has 48 seats, but Ra’am and another Arab-led party, the Joint List, recommended him to lead the government. The Joint List, however, is more unlikely to agree to any of Eisenkot’s demands, and therefore if it does support the prospective prime minister, it will be from outside the government.
Political jockeying continues in Israel, with other factors – such as who the ultra-Orthodox parties will back, and how many of Eisenkot’s coalition partners will be willing to accept any role for Ra’am – complicating matters.
Competing loyalties
During consultations with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on November 5, Abbas was asked why he would not use the “terrorist” designation when describing Hamas. The Ra’am leader said he needed the “space to be a bridge” between Jews and Palestinians.
“Leave me also a space to protect myself and my family,” he added, saying it was an issue of “life and death”.
Jabareen warned of underlying tensions even if an agreement over the designation was reached.
“There is also a security dispute,” Jabareen said. “Signing the classification of Hamas does not determine how Ra’am will act if the government decides to resume a wide war in Gaza.”
Then there is the question of recognising Israel as a Jewish state. Abbas has previously accepted that as a political reality, saying in 2021 that the country had been established as a Jewish state. But this year he clarified that accepting that as a reality did not mean endorsing it.
“The Jewish character of the state is an existing fact that was imposed on us, and we did not choose it,” he wrote in August.
Jabareen said Abbas was trying to navigate a complex situation, ensuring that he reflects the positions and beliefs of his Palestinian base, while being more acceptable and palatable to the wider Israeli public. The analyst, however, feels that this may have gone too far in the latter direction.
“Abbas is trying to be the most loyal to the government… he is looking at the Israeli voter more than he looks at his own voter,” Jabareen said. “He took legitimacy from his voter, and now he must see how he can correct the course with the Israeli voter.”
The prospect of Ra’am joining an Eisenkot government has also been seized upon by Netanyahu, who has repeatedly focused on the perceived threat of parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, portraying them as a danger to the state.
However, reports have emerged that Netanyahu’s close associate and former chief of staff, Natan Eshel, has contacted Abbas to gauge his stance on supporting Eisenkot.
“Publicly, Netanyahu is trying to make Ra’am’s support more politically costly for Eisenkot to secure, whether by encouraging opposition among Eisenkot’s partners or by making Abbas less willing to support him without concessions,” Jabareen said.
External support dilemma
Abbas’s options include joining Eisenkot’s coalition, supporting a minority government from outside, or joining the opposition.
“Supporting the government from outside it may reduce the cost of having an open partnership with Eisenkot, and give Abbas greater freedom to object to government decisions,” Jabareen said.
But there is another complication. Another leading member of Eisenkot’s bloc, Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, has repeatedly said he would oppose a minority government that is dependent on Arab-led parties.
Lieberman, a right-wing politician, has shown few signs of budging from his position, and has instead encouraged Eisenkot to partner with ultra-Orthodox parties – who were part of Netanyahu’s coalition during the last government – despite previous disputes over military conscription of Jewish religious students.
And then, even if Lieberman’s opposition is overcome, there is the potential for any future conflict, either with Palestinians or with regional states, to put any arrangement under strain, Jabareen warned.
“If it is just a short confrontation with Iran, then there is more of a chance of Abbas staying in any coalition,” Jabareen said. “But if it is a wider war in Gaza, or an escalation in Al-Aqsa or the West Bank, or even in Lebanon, that would put him under direct pressure from his supporters.”
Jabareen pointed to a similar dilemma in 2022, when Ra’am suspended its participation in the Israeli government coalition at the time over Israeli police raids and violence at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
“Would Ra’am stay silent on those issues just to keep the coalition together?” Jabareen asked. “I expect it would first voice its objections and, if the escalation continued, suspend its participation.”

noticias.titulo: Athletes rewrite the rules as Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics come to an end
noticias.resumen: Hosts Senegal thrive, and exuberant athletes defy the shadows cast over the Games by politics and history.
noticias.texto:
Athletes rewrite the rules as Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics come to an end
Hosts Senegal thrive, and exuberant athletes defy the shadows cast over the Games by politics and history.
Dakar, Senegal – At the last event of the Dakar Youth Olympics, sneakers shrieked across the floor as breakdancers faced off.
Baggy trousers carried national flags. B-boys and B-girls dropped into six-step footwork, spun through windmills and defied gravity in sudden freezes. Arms became legs, legs became arms, each move a challenge, each response a little more daring.
The competition on Friday, the last in the two-week games, was less about brute strength or speed than invention, creativity, balance and nerve. Each of the teenaged breakers was part gymnast, part basketballer, part boxer all at once, and they brought a fitting energy to the end of a Youth Olympics held on the world’s youngest continent.
Before Senegal became the first African country to host an Olympic event, France’s development agency lent the already heavily indebted West African country 80 million euros ($88m) for sporting facilities for the games. It came as young people across the region are increasingly questioning the former colonial power’s lingering influence.
At Dakar’s railway station, I watched French police helping secure the event. Above them stood a statue of two bronze soldiers – one African, the other French. The African one, named Demba, represents the colonial troops who fought and died for France during World War I. The French one, named Dupont, rests an arm on his shoulder, a gesture of fraternity that others see as colonial paternalism.
Beneath their gaze, politics and history still cast shadows over the games.
At the first swimming medal ceremony I attended, Russia’s 17-year-old Serafima Fokina stood on the podium, gold around her neck, singing her national anthem. Some spectators rose. Others remained seated.
For Russian athletes and their supporters, it was a moment of enormous symbolism: The Russian flag and anthem were back at an Olympic event for the first time since the country’s suspension after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Israel competed too despite its genocidal war on Gaza. A Senegalese man was arrested over a video opposing its participation that authorities described as threatening.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) insists on political neutrality, a principle it considers fundamental to the Olympic spirit.
“Youth athletes should not be held accountable for the actions of their governments,” the IOC said, arguing that sport offers them access to hope.
But neutrality is a delicate ideal in a world divided by war, and the flags they carried can never be separated from the conflicts beyond the podiums.
For Palestinian swimmer Alma Shaat, representing her country carried a different weight. She had a message for the children of Gaza.
“Any little girl in Palestine right now, specifically Gaza, I would tell her … to continue following her dreams,” she told me. “She’s not doing it only for herself, but she’s doing it for the people in Gaza and in Palestine.”
Senegal outperform France as China tops medal table
China ended up topping the medals table with 18 golds. Japan were second on 11 golds and Russia third with eight.
Eighty Senegalese athletes had travelled not to France or the United States but to China to train before the fames, part of China’s soft diplomacy. For Senegal it paid off – they finished sixth, five golds to their name, ahead of France.
At her final news conference of the games, International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry fought back tears. The Zimbabwean, who is the first African and first woman to lead the IOC, had helped bring the games to Dakar.
“I am so proud. I’m so grateful,” she said.
Yet it did not all go smoothly. At the Olympic village, the real test of unity came with the heat as athletes stayed in university dormitories without air-conditioning.
Outside the arenas, not everyone could get in. Events sold out. Transport was costly. But neighbourhood sports offered another way to join the celebrations in a city where children play football in the streets, and wrestlers train on the beach.
And sometimes divisions appeared to matter more than national pride.
I overheard a French-speaking Swiss journalist dismiss the prospect of covering a medal won by a German-speaking Swiss athlete. He also complained about the timing of events and the Olympic quota system, which limited participation to one athlete per country per event while giving greater representation to African nations.
But his complaints seemed strangely out of touch with the joyful spirit of the athletes, who were busy rewriting the rules. They had taken hold of the microphones and the cameras themselves. Each became a broadcaster, telling their stories through Instagram and TikTok, reaching audiences well beyond the television networks.
Back at the breakdancing finals, China’s Holy Rain faced Saturn of Chinese Taipei – two teenagers, one from mainland China, the other from Taiwan, dancing out their rivalry.
Amid the roar of the crowd, one spectator leaned towards another and shouted into his ear: “Imagine if their leaders could do the same.”
In the end, Japan’s Hiyo beat Ukraine’s 14-year-old Nikastar for the gold and Spain’s Mini Ali took bronze against Morocco’s Nawel.
Beneath their flags, rivals battled to the sound of hip-hop, then embraced. The flags remained. So did the divisions they represented. But for a few beats, neither seemed to matter.
