noticias.texto:
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot condemned a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens, after the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accused Arab parties of electoral fraud without evidence.
Netanyahu has repeatedly targeted Arab parties and Palestinian citizens of Israel after his party received a disappointing electoral showing, accusing them of manipulating the election and being linked to Hamas. Israeli electoral authorities have rejected these claims as not being backed by evidence.
Arab citizens of Israel, the vast majority of them of Palestinian descent, comprise more than 20% of the country’s population.
Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security branch, sought to question four Arab lawmakers, including the Arab-majority Ra’am party head, Mansour Abbas, leading to accusations that the security agency had become politicised.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story. The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis.
The statement also reflected political realities in Israel, as Arab parties found themselves kingmakers after the latest election. The two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured 19 seats in the October election.
They have the potential to help Eisenkot form a governing coalition and become Israel’s next prime minister. If Eisenkot cannot form a coalition within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, the mandate to form a government would pass to another lawmaker, potentially Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has to balance the competing interests of several parties if he hopes to form a coalition. Rightwing elements of the opposition have pledged to drop their support of the prospective PM if he cooperates with Arab parties.
His statement on Friday portrayed a more statesman-like approach to ruling than his more rightwing, demagogic opponents who have used Arab parties and citizens as political scapegoats over the last three years.
“[Arab citizens] have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Eisenkot said in his statement.
“The prime minister of Israel is the prime minister of all Israeli citizens, including those who did not vote for him,” he added.
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
In a speech, Netanyahu falsely claimed that the two Arab lists sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.
“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
Israeli media has reported that Eisenkot has also been reaching out to the country’s ultra-Orthodox parties for a potential alliance. The issue of the ultra-Orthodox not serving in the Israeli military was one of the hot button issues during the October election, with Eisenkot previously saying they should also be included in the country’s mandatory draft.

noticias.titulo: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
noticias.resumen: International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes. The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.
The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.
“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”
ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.
“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.
Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.
“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.
For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.
Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.
A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.
The former general is separately being investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.
For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.
The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.
However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.
Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

noticias.titulo: Two killed in Leeds after car pursued by police crashes into another vehicle
noticias.resumen: Four arrested after BMW collides with Volkswagen on Gelderd Road, with police appealing for witnesses Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested after the crash in Leeds on Sunday and appealed for witnesses to come forward. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police.
West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested after the crash in Leeds on Sunday and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
A force spokesperson said that at 12.44am a blue BMW 123D had failed to stop for a police vehicle in Gelderd Road, leading to a pursuit. The BMW then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco that was turning into Gelderd Road.
Police said the driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man from York, had been pronounced dead at the scene. A passenger in the same car, a 23-year-old woman from York, died in hospital a short time later. Neither has been formally named.
A 39-year-old man from Harrogate was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis in relation to the incident. He remains in custody.
Three other occupants of the BMW, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening. All three were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.
West Yorkshire police have referred themselves to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which has declared an independent investigation. A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We have started an independent investigation after a fatal road traffic collision in Leeds following a pursuit involving West Yorkshire police.
“After we were notified by West Yorkshire police, we declared an independent investigation at around 2.30am and sent investigators to the scene and police post-incident procedure to begin gathering evidence.
“Our inquiries are at a very early stage.”
The junction where the crash took place is surrounded by several car dealerships.
Pictures shared on social media overnight appeared to show an area around a segment of Gelderd Road cordoned off, with a fire engine and several police cars and ambulance vehicles in attendance. The pictures also appeared to show a dark car a short distance away from a very badly damaged white car just outside a used car dealership on Gelderd Road.
A cordon was still in place on Sunday morning with several officers in attendance, including a few inspecting the damaged cars. Drivers were advised to avoid the area.
Police appealed for witnesses and urged anyone with information or dashcam, mobile phone or CCTV footage to contact officers via 101 or online, quoting reference 13260649342.

noticias.titulo: Ethnic minority groups in Wales four times more likely to be target of police facial scans
noticias.resumen: Exclusive: South Wales police figures show BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, despite being 7% of population Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias. Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population . Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias.
Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population.
The force polices Wales’s largest cities – Cardiff and Swansea – and has pioneered several versions of AI-enabled facial recognition technology. The latest figures relate to police officers capturing a person’s face with a smartphone and running the image through an algorithm called “Neoface” to match it against custody mugshots and other face databases. Most scans are made because people are suspected of crimes.
Civil liberties campaigners called the ethnicity figures “alarming”. The force said they raised “concerns about disproportionality” and that it was reviewing its approach. The data relates to a full year of use in 2025 and was obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. Even when compared with arrest data for the police area, in which 11% of people arrested are from ethnic minorities, the face-scan figures appear disproportionate.
South Wales is one of the first UK constabularies to routinely use this “officer-initiated facial recognition” (OIFR) technology, which aims to identify suspects, wanted criminals and missing people who decline to give their details when challenged as well as people who are found unconscious, uncommunicative or dead. A similar system is being trialled by the Metropolitan police in London and has also been tested in Liverpool.
Critics have called facial recognition tools “Orwellian” and there have been repeated concerns about algorithmic bias putting ethnic minorities at greater risk of wrongful arrest. Last week, the police watchdog warned that innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, remained at risk of wrongful arrest if police treated inaccurate retrospective facial recognition data as evidence.
But advocates – including the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood – believe facial recognition is the biggest breakthrough for catching criminals since fingerprints and DNA matching. Other versions of the technology include live facial recognition cameras directed from marked vans and cameras fixed to lamp-posts, like those piloted in Croydon between October 2025 and March 2026, which led to 173 arrests, including of rape, kidnap and sexual assault suspects.
“This data shows that intrusive biometric tools are being used to disproportionately target minority communities,” said Jake Hurfurt, the head of research and investigations at Big Brother Watch, a civil liberties campaign that obtained the figures. “It is alarming that non-white people have been subject to face scans at a much higher rate than would be expected either by the region’s demography or the makeup of people arrested in the region.”
Aliya Mohammed, the chief executive of Race Equality First, a Cardiff-based anti-discrimination organisation, said the figures raised “serious concerns about racial disproportionality”.
“Facial recognition is not neutral because it uses AI,” she said. “If existing biases influence who is stopped and scanned, technology can reinforce and even amplify inequality.”
Alvi Choudhury, 26, who was arrested in February for a burglary in a city he had never visited after police face-scanning software confused him with another person of south Asian heritage on a custody database, said it was “very concerning” that ethnic minorities were being disproportionately scanned.
“The police are under pressure to solve crimes and they are over-reliant on these AI tools,” he said. “They shouldn’t be arresting people based on the AI tools alone.”
He remained worried AI systems were not trained on enough ethnic minority faces to ensure the number of false positives was no greater than for white people.
According to the data for 2025, South Wales police officers initiated face scans of 257 adults and 14 children, including two under-10s. More than half were suspected of a crime, being unlawfully at large or breaching bail conditions. The next most common reasons were because officers believed the person posed a risk of harm to themselves or others – such as stalkers or sex offenders. In about one in 10 cases, a scan was initiated for a suspected missing person while the technology was used to identify a dead person about once a fortnight.
In many of the cases, the scan failed to deliver a match or the subject agreed to share their identity. Where a match was made, arrests followed in 48% of cases and no further action resulted in a third of cases.
A spokesperson for South Wales police said: “We recognise the figures raise concerns about disproportionality. The number of OIFR searches remains relatively small, and the use of the technology is in its infancy. That said, each deployment is based on the individual circumstances that officers are dealing with at that time and is subject to supervisory and force-wide scrutiny.”
They said the force would “continue to review our approach through our established governance processes, which also include input from independent advisory groups and external scrutiny panels” and added: “Where opportunities for learning or improvement are identified, we will take appropriate action.”
Earlier this month, the Home Office announced a new facial recognition watchdog with the power to stop police forces using the technology if they fail to follow rules and new laws in the police reform bill, including a duty for the use of face scans to be intelligence-led and proportionate.
The Home Office said decisions on the operational use of facial recognition were matters for the police, but they must comply with equality, human rights and data protection laws and its use must be necessary, proportionate and fair.

noticias.titulo: Poundland pins rescue hopes on Yorkshire Tea, Pot Noodle and Gloria Gaynor
noticias.resumen: Chain restocks stores in operation named after singer of I Will Survive after US owners release funds Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government. In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government.
In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend.
The name comes from the Gloria Gaynor song I Will Survive, which soundtracked a defiant video posted by Poundland on social media showing pallets of Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles making their way from depots to the shelves.
Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm MPs have accused of “predatory capitalism”, earlier agreed to unlock £21m of £50m that it had been accused of endangering the business by withholding.
The money will provide breathing space while rescue talks continue, ensuring that suppliers continue sending goods to branches during the crucial pre-Christmas trading period.
Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of last month, throwing the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers into uncertainty.
Last week the chain won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors, giving it until 26 November to find a buyer.
The company and Gordon Brothers are now heading for a frantic period of talks with potential buyers and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.
Discussions could be soured by allegations – denied by Gordon Brothers – that the US investment group is more interested in protecting its own interests by breaking up the business despite signs of a dramatic improvement in its trading performance.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1 and claims to have rescued the company from collapse when nobody else would.
However, the US business has faced criticism from MPs, who have accused it of extracting millions of pounds as Poundland found itself on a knife-edge.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business select committee, has likened Gordon Brothers to “the wolf of Wall Street, on the British high street”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers has denied freezing any funds that should have been available to Poundland and pointed to loans that it has provided to prop up the company.
Reynolds plans to meet Poundland and Gordon Brothers before the deadline to stave off administration runs out, according to a report by Sky News.
He and Andy Burnham have expressed concerns about Gordon Brothers’ conduct, with the prime minister asking why the US company has yet to accept an offer for a business that employs 11,000 people.
Poundland has said it is in discussions with three potential buyers.
Bids from the investment groups Xyra Group Holdings and Innovest are understood to have relatively little chance of success.
Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish company, is Poundland’s preferred bidder but progress has stalled over the repayment terms of a loan from Gordon Brothers.
A number of high-street retailers, including Tesco, are eyeing up some of Poundland’s shops.
A Gordon Brothers spokesperson said: “Funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.
“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.”
The Guardian approached Poundland for comment. The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade declined to comment.

noticias.titulo: Cold and health alerts issued for Scotland and northern England as snow and ice expected
noticias.resumen: UKHSA warns of health impact on those vulnerable to cold and urges people to check in with neighbours Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, and alerts for the risk to health services are due to begin on Sunday evening. The Met Office issued yellow weather warnings for ice for central and eastern Scotland from 6pm on Sunday evening until 10am on Monday. People should be vigilant as they travelled, due to the risk from slipping on footpaths in icy conditions, it added. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, and alerts for the risk to health services are due to begin on Sunday evening.
The Met Office issued yellow weather warnings for ice for central and eastern Scotland from 6pm on Sunday evening until 10am on Monday. People should be vigilant as they travelled, due to the risk from slipping on footpaths in icy conditions, it added.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) meanwhile issued yellow cold health alerts for north-west and north-east England and for Yorkshire and the Humber about the impact of the cold snap on health services. A previous warning for the West Midlands has been dropped.
The warnings will come into force at 9pm on Sunday and run until Thursday morning.
The UKHSA alerts meant the weather was “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, the agency said.
Suffolk had the lowest temperature in the UK overnight into Sunday, with -4.5C recorded at Santon Downham.
The Met Office said snow could fall on hills in northern England and Scotland in the coming days.
Dan Stroud, the senior operational meteorologist at the Met Office, said the cold weather was caused by northerly winds and longer nights.
Further weather warnings could be issued early in the week, the Met Office indicated. The weather will become briefly milder in midweek before returning to cold as the weekend approaches.
Stroud said: “The weather does try and settle down a little later in the period, with high pressure trying to build in from the middle of the week onwards from the north.
“So it will be turning brighter, but still plenty of showers in the mix. It will remain cold in the north, with temperatures remaining near average in the south.”
He added: “There will be a cold, widespread frost in the north on Friday, with daytime temperatures below normal, in single digits.”
Paul Coleman, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold health alert of the season, and we can expect more as we move further into winter.
“Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.”
Coleman added that people should try to heat the rooms they used the most, if possible, and dress warmly during colder spells.

noticias.titulo: Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit
noticias.resumen: From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair? For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries. But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.
But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.
Dupes are products that claim to offer a similar experience to a high-end item though do not claim to be that product. They were originally a Gen Z obsession but have become a mainstream shopping trend at a time of strained household finances.
“No matter what age you are, how much money you’ve got to spend, everyone wants to ‘luxe it up’ with a dupe,” says Catherine Shuttleworth, a retail consultant and chief executive of Savvy Marketing.
“The message is ‘why not be smart like me saving cash but still looking good’,” she says.
“In the case of homewares, a high street dupe of a luxury branded candle can look and smell just as good as the real thing, and will your visitors really notice that your table lamps are from B&M not the White Company?”
Dupe culture is being supercharged by social media, particularly TikTok. More than 30 million people across the UK now use TikTok each month, according to the company, with Gen-Z’ers admitting that seeing products sell out or go viral makes them more likely to buy them.
Data firm YPulse has been tracking consumer attitudes to dupes for several years and Tori D’Amico, managing content editor, says: “The idea that a dupe can be a true replacement for a luxury item is still prevalent. Dupes are not shameful or embarrassing to own. Young consumers brag online about finding a good deal and share it with the masses.”
YPulse’s most recent research found that 44% of UK 13- to 39-year-olds have bought a dupe in the past year. When asked, just over half (53%) of this age group agreed that “the quality of dupe/fake luxury items makes me less likely to want to purchase a real luxury item”.
Dupes are particularly prominent in the beauty world but are also found in other sectors including food, furniture, homeware and designer fashion.
US “dupe” retailer Quince, which sells upmarket products ranging from candles to cashmere sweaters, has just launched in the UK. Alongside each product on its website it suggests the saving you are making against more expensive brands. A £50 woman’s red cashmere jumper, for example, is pictured alongside graphics comparing it with jumpers from Cos and Reiss costing three times as much.
Fragrance, in particular, is a popular target. There are more than 50,000 videos on TikTok under the combined hashtag #perfumedupe and #perfumedupes, where influencers rate imitation fragrances against famous names and tell viewers where to find them.
With fragrances a sought-after Christmas gift the platform is awash with content extolling these cheaper scents. Instead of spending nearly £130 on Mugler’s Alien try Zara’s Violet Blossom for £15.99, suggests one. Or, if you can’t afford Le Labo’s Another 13, try Marks & Spencer’s Aura Ambrette, a snip at £22.50.
In TikTok Dupeland budget supermarket Aldi is lauded as a perfume house with its Lacura brand tipped to offer substitutes for high-end favourites ranging from Paradoxe to Flowerbomb and Baccarat Rouge – for £7 a bottle.
“These cut-price products are in focus right now as consumers look for cheaper alternatives in response to rising prices,” says Eric Mills from market research firm NielsenIQ. In a recent survey, 38% of UK consumers said that in the past 12 months they had switched to lower-priced brands to manage their shopping bills.
“The buyers of these brands are often thought of as only younger consumers, but while Gen Z are key spenders, it’s millennials who account for the greatest proportion of sales,” he adds.
In a microcosm of what is likely happening elsewhere in the market, the number of people buying dupe fragrances online is up 17% in the past year which is ahead of the overall market.
With the continued adoption of AI tools, Mills says: “It’s easy to imagine dupes gaining further traction, as consumers can simply ask a chatbot for a cheaper alternative to their favourite luxury scent.”
With dupes copying well-known brands without pretending to be the real thing they occupy a space somewhere between authentic and fake. While consumers might love dupes, the targets are less enthusiastic.
Celebrity makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury, whose £350m fortune stems from the sale of her eponymous beauty empire to Spanish fragrance and fashion group Puig, recently told the BBC that “when you dupe, you dupe the consumer”.
“It is not Charlotte Tilbury … and it is not performing the way that my products do,” Tilbury says of cheaper imitations. “If I could do them for those prices I would.”
Charlotte Tilbury has had some success pushing back and, in 2019, brought a successful copyright case against Aldi over the designs on its Filmstar Bronze & Glow palette which the supermarket had copied.
Claire Breheny, partner and head of trade marks at Mathys & Squire suggests that business owners should be requesting that dupes be taken down from online platforms or social media. Brand owners “need to protect their packaging and get-up, not just their name.
“The risk for consumers is that similar packaging doesn’t guarantee similar quality, ingredients or performance – although a cheaper alternative isn’t necessarily always going to be inferior.”
With the cost of living crisis only making dupes more attractive to shoppers, Savvy Marketing’s Shuttleworth says that nearly 80% of shoppers its survey polled were happy to selectively spend more on treats and luxuries where they think it’s worth it.
“The challenge for top brands like Charlotte Tilbury, is that they need to be able to convince shoppers the quality difference is always worth paying for.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes
noticias.resumen: Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes. Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access
noticias.texto:
Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.
Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.
The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center.
In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times.
Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”.
In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda.
Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”.
Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends.
“Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.”
Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.”
For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship.
Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters.
The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns.
In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.
Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”.
Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”.
Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order. In late September, a federal appeals court for the 11th circuit rejected a request from Trump and his lawyers to immediately lift sanctions that Williams imposed in response to the settlement Trump and the DoJ backed over the leak of his tax returns.
In its ruling, the appeals court denied a request by two Trump lawyers, Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein, to pause sanctions against them over their handling of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS. The court ruled the lawyers had not demonstrated they would succeed in challenging finding that they acted in bad faith.
In another legal blow for Trump, two restraining orders were issued in October by district judge Jennifer Rochon in New York to stop his use of public funds for financing campaign style ads after Campaign Legal Center Action representing Common Cause, along with Public Integrity Project Action and Democracy Forward sued.
In her second emergency order on 30 October, Judge Rochon ruled that three ads could no longer run using government funds on Instagram and two other sites since they were “purely partisan” .
One of the ads echoed Trump’s dubious claim that if Republicans maintained control of Congress, all Americans would receive $5,000. The three ads Rochon ordered removed were headlined “$5,000 to Americans” the “Cost of Socialism” and “Every Democrat Voted against No Tax on Tips”.
Shortly before Rochon’s first ruling, Trump in a Truth Social post on 5 October defended using government funds for the ads and blithely stated that tapping public funds was “rather standard”.
But with growing criticism, including from some Republicans, Trump announced he would pay for them himself from his political fundraising operation. The justice department also tried to forestall the first restraining order by asserting that “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow”.
Renata O’Donnell, a senior legal counsel with Campaign Legal Center who worked on the case, told the Guardian: “The Department of Homeland Security used $20m in taxpayer dollars to pay a private ad agency for airtime for government-created propaganda. This is blatantly illegal.”
O’Donnell added: “In direct violation of the law, White House staff, whose salaries are paid with taxpayer dollars, were creating propaganda, including ads that promised people $5,000 to vote Republican.”
In another pending legal battle that courts have yet to rule on, Democracy Defenders Fund filed a lawsuit with the San Francisco city attorney, the Washington Litigation Group and Platkin LLP to block a Trump financial gambit to offer special early access to his Truth Social posts to users who pay a fee as high as $100,000 per month to the parent company of Truth Social.
The lawsuit was filed in mid-September against Trump Media and Technology Group, which operates and owns Truth Social.
San Francisco city attorney David Chiu asked the San Francisco superior court to bar Trump Media from offering its new service, dubbed “Trump API”, or a similar one, plus provide monetary damages for violating the public trust and the state’s unfair competition law.
“Trump Media created a marketplace that enables insider trading, which Trump directly profits from,” Chiu said in a statement. “This scheme turns the public trust into private profit. It is corruption, plain and simple.”
A Trump Media spokesperson ridiculed the lawsuit when it was filed, charging that “the people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the leftwing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information”.
David Ogden, a senior counsel with DDF who has worked on the case, noted that “Congress made clear that the president, like any public servant, shouldn’t be permitted to profiteer off of special access to government information. It’s a violation of the public trust and it’s important that it be stopped.”
In the eyes of Barbara McQuade, former US attorney for eastern Michigan, who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, the different court rulings against Trump’s financial ploys reveal his penchant for “personal enrichment” and political ploys during his presidency.
“It seems that Trump has no shame about using his office for personal enrichment. We can’t count on his own conscience, ethics or advisers to check his worst instincts, but the courts have seen through his various schemes, from his slush fund to his use of taxpayer funds for political ads.”

noticias.titulo: Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’
noticias.resumen: Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the
noticias.texto:
The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks.
Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy’s longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits.
Kennedy and his allies have also profited from growing misinformation peddled through books, paid speaking events and the supplement industry.
“I do think he’s a real ideologue – he really believes in this,” said Dorit Reiss, professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. But Kennedy and his allies are likely “very happy to make money doing it”, she said.
Peter Hotez, professor and dean of Baylor College of Medicine’s National School of Tropical Medicine, agreed, saying Kennedy’s actions are likely a combination of “being an ideological zealot and making money either for himself or for his associates”.
Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said the department “categorically reject claims that Secretary Kennedy is pursuing personal gain or seeking to dismantle American medicine”.
Prior to his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy disclosed $2.5m in income from referrals for vaccine-related lawsuits. In the hearing, Kennedy would not commit to forgoing compensation from vaccine lawsuits after he leaves office. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, listed several ways in which Kennedy’s actions, some of which have now happened, could influence future litigation.
“Kennedy can kill off access to vaccines and make millions of dollars while he does it,” Warren said at the hearing. “Kids might die. But Robert Kennedy can keep cashing in.” She pointed to Kennedy’s involvement in litigation against Merck for its HPV vaccine – lawsuits that were settled for more than $50m in June 2026. After the confirmation hearing, Kennedy said his son would receive the money, expected to be 10% of the total; it’s unclear if he did.
“For most of us, money going to our children isn’t exactly money not going to us,” Reiss said. “There’s a dozen ways he and his family could benefit” from Kennedy’s actions, she added.
Kennedy has long profited from his anti-vaccine misinformation. Tony Lyons, Kennedy’s publisher and a central figure in the constellation of Maha political organizations, reportedly paid Kennedy $4m in book advances over the past year. The publisher also paid Kennedy $451,000 in consulting fees before he became HHS secretary. That’s on top of other book sales and paid speaking engagements over the years. Kennedy also earned $326,000 for the 15 weeks he served as chairman of Children’s Health Defense in 2023 – more than half of his $510,000 salary in 2022.
More recently, he received free flights and trips on a yacht from a former donor to his presidential campaign, who is now under investigation by the Senate for the gifts totaling some $250,000.
As HHS secretary, Kennedy has also loosened regulations on peptides, a booming part of the largely unregulated wellness industry.
“I think he’s doing what everyone knew he was going to do,” said Hotez. Kennedy, before and during his tenure as leader of HHS, has been “chipping away at public confidence in vaccines and immunizations in favor of products that can be sold by the wellness industry”, he added.
Aaron Siri, Kennedy’s former lawyer who represents people who say they have experienced severe side effects, has advocated for changing all vaccines to “shared clinical decision-making”. If those changes took place, Siri could argue that the vaccines are not covered under the VICP and therefore open to litigation.
“A lot of what he is doing is geared toward setting up a more profitable litigation atmosphere,” Reiss said.
Siri did not respond to the Guardian’s question about profiting from litigation, but instead argued that “if vaccines are as ‘safe’ as touted by the government, then there should be no need for immunity to liability and, likewise, there should be very few, if any, successful cases”.
The most common claim to VICP – making up more than half – has to do with where the vaccine is administered, not the vaccines themselves.
The VICP was established in 1986 in order to expedite compensation for anyone who experienced adverse side effects from vaccines. There are real costs to undermining the program, Reiss said. It’s very rare for people to develop severe side effects after vaccination, but when they do, they should be compensated, she said. But if false claims about vaccine harms proliferate, they will obscure those with legitimate claims.
Filing a VICP claim is an easier process than winning a lawsuit, which takes time and effort and also demands a higher burden of proof.
“That’s why the whole vaccine injury system was set up,” Hotez said. “It was actually to the plaintiff’s benefit to get a faster judgment without having to show detailed evidence of proof.”
Without VICP, patients would need to pay lawyers a large chunk of their settlements, if their case moves through the courts at all, Reiss said: “The lack of contingency fee means they don’t have to pay 30% to 50% of their earnings through the lawyer.”
Compensating doctors for reporting side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) risks offering “the wrong incentives” to unscrupulous providers who could increase such activities to become a new revenue source, Reiss said.
The changes could “certainly” be used by organizations such as Children’s Health Defense to legitimize its work spreading misinformation “and convince donors and others that they should give them more money”, she added.
VAERS, alongside several other vaccine monitoring systems, works well to pick up signals of very rare side effects, such as myocarditis from initial mRNA Covid vaccines and thrombotic thrombocytopenia in the Johnson and Johnson Covid vaccine, Hotez noted. But it’s not built to prove links between vaccines and certain side effects, as vaccination opponents have attempted to do, he said.
“The VAERS system was never meant to show cause and effect,” Hotez said. “It’s like looking for signs of alien communication in outer space. You look at every little blip, and almost all of them have nothing, are not real. But you have to analyze them.”
Years ago, Hotez engaged Kennedy in a series of conversations about misinformation that autism spectrum disorder is related to vaccines. Hotez pointed to known environmental influences on autism, like the anti-seizure medication valproic acid. Kennedy “had no interest then; he has no interest now”, Hotez said. “Even back then, there was a heavy emphasis on being a plaintiff attorney and suing vaccine companies. So that’s his narrow interest, which has nothing to do with reality – and he’s still going by the same playbook.”
Kennedy has attacked medical journals and schools, and funding for medical research has fallen sharply under his leadership. Such actions appear intended to “completely wipe out American medicine as we know it in favor of this whole system of grifting and pseudoscience”, Hotez said.

noticias.titulo: Black voters helped Democrats win in Georgia. Now they expect to be heard
noticias.resumen: Activists have been shouting about economic issues for years – in January they will expect lawmakers to respond Stonecrest is resolutely middle class. noticias.texto:
Stonecrest is resolutely middle class. About six out of 10 of its voters cast ballots in the 2026 election and about 90% of them voted for Democrats, according to election figures. And they have often been overlooked by Georgia’s Republican establishment.
The fundraiser Keisha Lance Bottoms held at the Privi event center and retreat in suburban Atlanta in September didn’t draw a lot of attention. But Stonecrest, by one measure the largest city in the United States with a non-Hispanic Black population above 90%, tends to roll under the radar.
It’s infuriating, said Vaughn Irons, Privi’s founder. “I think she came to speak to a community that often gets driven through and flown over.”
Black voting power helped secure victory for US Senator Jon Ossoff, Bottoms’ run for the governor’s race and a slew of down-ballot candidates. Now, those voters expect to be heard.
Culture war issues come with the change in partisan control of Georgia’s government; on abortion, on guns and on LGBTQ+ rights. But the customary politics of Georgia start and end with business, and that attitude is bipartisan.
Georgia’s Black voters have long wrestled with the Black Mecca paradox. Atlanta has long attracted Black professional talent from across the country and the world who were looking for strong African American political and cultural institutions and an economic environment perceived to give Black people an even shake.
But upward mobility for native-born Black Atlantans has been anemic. Black unemployment rates are lower in Atlanta than the nation overall. Georgia leads the nation for Black executive representation and recent income growth. But Georgia offers the worst chances for wealth of any state for a Black child born into poverty.
Activists have stood on soapboxes to shout at Georgia’s lawmakers about these economic issues for the last 20 years. In January, those voters will expect their government to answer them.
The opinions of Black voters – particularly Black women – have been ignored for years, said Tiffani Stephens, a voter in DeKalb county. “We’re taken as the pretty person and all we care about is clothes, shoes and makeup,” she said. “Where if you really know a Black woman, you know these are additives. We are of substance. Deep substance.”
Democrats didn’t just win the marquee political contests in Georgia this November. They won every statewide election from the lieutenant governor’s office down to the insurance commissioner. Democrats displaced a Republican majority on the electricity rate-setting public service commission. Almost all the statewide office holders will be Black women, including the incoming speaker of the Georgia house, state representative Carolyn Hugley of Columbus. Democrats are one state senator short of controlling both chambers.
“This was not just a magical thing. This took a long time, building the infrastructure for the south and particularly for Georgia,” said Deborah Scott, executive director of Georgia STAND-UP, a “think and act tank” non-profit advocating for job training and economic development for working families.
It has taken multiple failed election cycles, chipping away at layers of cynicism, to be ready for this moment, Scott said. Stacey Abrams, two-time gubernatorial candidate turned democracy activist, deserves some credit for Georgia’s political results in November. But it is also the product of meticulous relationship-building groundwork, particularly by organizations led by Black women, she added.
“If Stacey is the tree that all of these newly elected officials are sitting in, then the roots of that are community-based organizations and non-profit organizations like Georgia STAND-UP and the People’s Agenda, folks that have been doing the work for a long time.”
Describing the election results as a referendum on gas prices, or the war, or Donald Trump, is reductive, Scott said. Black voters assess their conditions holistically. “It’s not just about the gas prices are too damn high – which is true – but it’s also about the quality of life for regular Americans.”
The last two years have been radicalizing for some Georgia voters, Scott said. While highly-educated CDC employees found themselves impaled on the spear tips of HHS secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, nonprofits serving low-income communities like Scott’s have been scrambling to replace federal spending and a dearth of private grants, she said.
Before the election, activists have been squabbling for scarce resources, she said. Today, they are bathing in the afterglow of political unity.
For 20 years, Democrats have been shut out of major decisions about Georgia’s policy direction. The state has restrictive abortion laws and libertine gun laws. It is one of 10 states which did not expand access to Medicaid.
It has also attracted stunning amounts of foreign investment during Kemp’s two-terms in office, with car manufacturers, battery plants and chip makers locating to Georgia. But almost all of that state-directed economic development landed either in the north Georgia foothills or in rural south Georgia, like the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America manufacturing hub in Bryan county, rewarding white, Republican voters with jobs and political attention.
Scott speaks about the urgent need to encode voting rights protections in the Georgia constitution with one breath. In the next, she talks about deepening the port of Savannah, or the new Audi car plant being built near Macon.
“If you look at rural Georgia versus urban and suburban Georgia, it really is a tale of two states,” she said. “This is an opportunity for economic development in all of the regions around Georgia … it’s an opportunity to equalize the state. It’s Atlanta and the rest of the state. And of course, even in Atlanta, it’s the tale of two cities. Those that are born poor will not come out of it. There’s an opportunity for really affordable housing and real economic development.”
The city of Stonecrest, a suburb of south-eastern Atlanta, exists as a municipality because its Black, middle-class voters decided 10 years ago that they wanted their community to incorporate to serve them the way white middle-class voters are served 30 miles north in Sandy Springs. They wanted political leadership that matched their aspirations.
“As a small business owner, which I am, this is an opportunity to have a seat at the table,” said Kazemde Ajamu, who owns Akoma Coffee & Books at Stonecrest.
Ajamu is looking for Georgia to recognize microbusinesses and to better empower entrepreneurship for small business owners. “I feel good about the incoming governor-elect, that this gives us an opportunity to have a voice to speak to it, to create laws that help micro-businesses, mom-and-pops … That’s one example of having a seat at the table, having a voice, and someone that’s listening and can be proactive in that area.”
While Democrats have control over the apparatus of state government, there is no reason to believe that’s a permanent condition. Political competition will force Bottoms and the state legislature to pay attention everywhere, Irons said.
“Everybody’s interest is in growing, and having prosperity and better education,” Irons said. “The success of what’s likely to happen for the next governor is to create an environment where all parties that are serious about the growth and the prosperity of the state of Georgia can have a seat at the table.”
The accession of Bottoms as governor and Democrats in control of government agencies may mean that a place like Stonecrest is less likely to be overlooked, Irons said. But the former HUD official and economic development director for DeKalb county said that doesn’t alone solve problems.
“I think every community has to be ready for the investment that it wants,” Irons said. “And so you have a governor that you can access differently. I think Governor [Brian] Kemp probably was aware of the needs, but a different group of people had access, right? I think now that just because you have access doesn’t mean you don’t have your own responsibility to be ready.”

noticias.titulo: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
noticias.resumen: Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight. The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.
Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.
“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.
“Making more believers by the day,” wrote Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa.
SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. Musk has touted the rocket’s reusability as a way to reel in the enormous costs of space travel.
Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.
Starship’s advances have also aided the expansion of Musk’s satellite internet empire. The spacecraft deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites during this recent flight.

noticias.titulo: Evacuation zone lifted after bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant
