WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."
The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."
Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."
Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."
The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."
The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue," it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."
Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. "We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," she said. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."
The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on "any and all Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"
Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behavior" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.

noticias.titulo: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
noticias.resumen: Some college football games were delayed a few hours on Saturday or postponed to Sunday. And in Oklahoma at least, there will be perks for fans to make up for the inconvenience, including cheap beers.
noticias.texto:
FAA ground stop disrupts college football
The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.
Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.
"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."
Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.
While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.
Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.
In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

noticias.titulo: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
noticias.resumen: A new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives has prompted Delray Beach to cancel its St. Patrick's Day parade after a nearly 60-year run.
noticias.texto:
Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.
The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.
The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.
The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.
In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.
"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.
The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.
If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.
"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."
Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.
Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.
"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."
The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.
"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."
The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.
"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

noticias.titulo: Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary
noticias.resumen: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy points blame toward contractor in explaining Friday's nation-wide aviation ground stop.
noticias.texto:
Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary
Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground, says Transportation Secretary
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy points blame toward contractor in explaining Friday's nation-wide aviation ground stop.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
What caused the cascade of failures which brought the U.S. air travel system to its knees on Friday? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation - a contractor was replacing a router to upgrade the nation's outdated air traffic control equipment when something went very wrong.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
SEAN DUFFY: This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment. Our contractor didn't meet the moment. Or the equipment didn't meet the moment and cause the outages.
SCHMITZ: The system is back online, and flights are now taking off, but travelers throughout the country are still dealing with the disruption. NPR spoke to one traveler, Andres Martinez Murillo, last night.
ANDRES MARTINEZ MURILLO: My flight keeps getting delayed further. They don't know if it's, like, a crew issue. They don't know if it's, like, a pilot issue. I don't even know if we have a plane.
SCHMITZ: Murillo told NPR he finally boarded his first flight this morning, but his second flight's been canceled, and he still does not know when he will reach his final destination. For more, we're joined by NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose. Hey, Joel.
JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Hey, Rob.
SCHMITZ: So many angry passengers today that still have not gotten to their destinations - what more do we know about the cause of all of this?
ROSE: We are starting to get a clearer picture. The heads of the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration held a press conference today, and they put the blame squarely on a longtime FAA contractor, L3 Harris Technologies. They say the company was doing a routine maintenance upgrade of a server as part of a transition from older copper wire to fiber optic cable, and that is when things went sideways.
Sean Duffy and FAA leaders were asked several times why a faulty router could lead to telecom outages across such a wide part of the country. They said that is still under investigation. In a statement, L3 Harris says it is supporting the FAA's investigation into what went wrong and that it takes the impact on airlines and travelers seriously.
SCHMITZ: OK. Let's step back here just for a moment. What was happening in the air while all of this was playing out on the ground?
ROSE: Air traffic controllers were starting to see intermittent problems with radar and communication systems around 3:30 p.m. Eastern. By 3:44 p.m., the FAA declared a nationwide ground stop. Here is some of the reaction from air traffic controllers and pilots in Salt Lake City, as you can hear in archived audio from the website, liveatc.net.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: You guys got any updates from your company about what's going on?
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Not at all. If you've got info, we're all ears.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: I wish we did. We basically only know what the FAA tells us, which is not a lot.
ROSE: I talked to one air traffic controller who was working when the outage began. He is a controller at one of the en route centers that handle high altitude traffic and was not authorized to speak publicly, but he described the situation as chaos. He said, a lot of airplanes were being diverted away from their original destinations. Some of them were running out of fuel. And he emphasized just how this whole system depends on the air traffic controllers, who found a way to more than 3,000 planes onto the ground quickly and safely, even when their equipment was letting them down.
SCHMITZ: So we've got a lot of confused pilots, a lot of confused air traffic controllers. You know, I'm just curious, the air traffic controller that you spoke to - did he have any thoughts about the apparent cause of this ground stop?
ROSE: I should say that we spoke this morning before the press conference by DOT, but this controller was already beginning to think that this was probably a mistake by a contractor who was doing work to upgrade the air traffic control system, which this controller says is happening all the time. He also places some of the blame on the oversight of the FAA for not having enough redundant systems in place, you know, to prevent this kind of outage from happening. He questioned why this work was going on in the middle of a busy Friday afternoon instead...
SCHMITZ: Right.
ROSE: ...Of late at night when it would not have had as much impact if something went wrong. He said it, quote, "just screams incompetence, like, gross incompetence."
SCHMITZ: You know, it does seem quite remarkable that a single point of failure like this could have such an enormous impact. What has the FAA said about this?
ROSE: Well, they said this was considered routine maintenance work. They are still investigating why it appears to have basically broken the entire national airspace. Here is Rebecca Guy, the acting chief technology officer at the FAA.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
REBECCA GUY: What we are doing is that root cause analysis, but at this time, we do believe what occurred with that router has been worked through.
ROSE: In other words, they think they have solved the problem. The FAA administrator promised that things should be back to normal by close of business on Sunday.
SCHMITZ: That is NPR transportation correspondent, Joel Rose. Joel, thank you so much for all that reporting.
ROSE: You're welcome.

noticias.titulo: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
noticias.resumen: The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, according to researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations at the Pan American Health Organization.
noticias.texto:
US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.
Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.
PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.
In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.
"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.
"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.
Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.
States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.
PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.
Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.
But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.
For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.
After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."
Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."
Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.
Past administrations sounded alarms
For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.
That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.
Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.
Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.
Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.
When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.
When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.
Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.
"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.
People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.
It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.
"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"
National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.
In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.
"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.
Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."
And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. "The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."
'The dog didn't bark'
Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.
Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."
Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.
"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."
Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.
"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.
"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.
Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.
More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.
The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.
CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.
"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."
The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.
Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.
The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."
The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.
Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.
Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.
When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.
Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.
At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.
To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.
"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

noticias.titulo: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
noticias.resumen: The company's spacecraft returned to its Texas launchpad in dramatic fashion — by carefully lowering itself until two metal arms attached to the launch tower could secure it.
noticias.texto:
SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.
"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.
SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.
It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

noticias.titulo: Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations
noticias.resumen: The bomb was discovered Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables plant in Peoria. Officials say the bomb has been "rendered safe," but called it a "credible threat." The FBI is investigating.
noticias.texto:
Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations
A bomb was found near an ethanol plant in central Illinois, sparking evacuations of those who live near the industrial site as law enforcement officials investigate, authorities said Saturday.
The bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. While officials say the device has since been "rendered safe," as of Saturday morning, all residents within a 1-mile radius remained under an evacuation notice as officials continued to scour the facility for any other bombs and evidence.
Meanwhile, shelters have been set up for those displaced by the threat, authorities said.
"This is a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters just after midnight Saturday. "We need to take the blast radius seriously."
FBI Special Agent Ryan Pressley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.
"We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," he said.
No arrests have been made at this time and no injuries have been reported.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."
It's not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don't result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.
"We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests," said Dixon. "We're asking for the public's patience while we work to make this area safe."
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.

noticias.titulo: Estonian drone maker targeted by 'GRU-ordered' sabotage attempt, PM says
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia was preparing to potentially close its border with Russia to "reduce the risks to our people and national security."
noticias.texto:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia was preparing to potentially close its border with Russia to "reduce the risks to our people and national security."
Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems was the target of a Russian intelligence-ordered sabotage attack on Saturday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
The attempted attack, which took place in the early hours of Saturday morning, aimed to cause an explosion and set fire to Threod's premises, according to Estonia's Internal Security Service.
In a post on social media on Sunday, Michal said "extensive damage" had been averted thanks to "heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement."
The alleged attackers have been detained, he added. Local media outlets are reporting that eight people were taken into custody in relation to the incident.
"This is part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal wrote.
Founded in 2012, Threod develops and manufactures unmanned aircraft and surveillance systems such as its Eos drones and eOpic electro-optical units. The company is based in Viimsi Parish, near the Estonian capital, Tallinn.
The Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, or GRU, is Russia's military intelligence agency, and it is suspected of being behind numerous hybrid attacks on European territory in recent years.
It is believed that the agency, along with other intelligence bodies in Russia, often attempts to recruit local assets to carry out sabotage missions.
Michal said Estonia was now preparing to potentially close its border with Russia to "reduce the risks to our people and national security."
It comes after Milrem Robotics, another Estonian defence firm, was hit by an arson attack in August. Estonian officials have said that attack was ordered by Russian special services.
Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Estonia and its Baltic neighbours have been particularly exposed to security consequences believed to stem from Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and there have been rapidly increasing reports of cyberattacks, drone incursions and sabotage attempts targeting the region.

noticias.titulo: Southeast Asian nations sign digital trade deal to ease payments and cut paperwork
noticias.resumen: Online shopping and digital services are growing across Southeast Asia, but businesses still face different rules in each country. ASEAN’s new agreement aims to make it easier to sell, receive payments and share data across the region.
noticias.texto:
Online shopping and digital services are growing across Southeast Asia, but businesses still face different rules in each country. ASEAN’s new agreement aims to make it easier to sell, receive payments and share data across the region.
Southeast Asian nations signed an agreement on Saturday aimed at making it easier for businesses to trade online, make payments and transfer data across borders.
The Digital Economy Framework Agreement was signed by ministers in Manila. It is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) first stand-alone, legally binding agreement on the digital economy.
It is due to take effect in May 2027, 180 days after signing, and replace the bloc’s 2019 agreement on electronic commerce, according to Singapore’s trade ministry.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. formally handed the signed agreement to ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn at the opening of the bloc’s summit on Sunday.
The pact promotes wider acceptance of electronic invoices, shipping documents and signatures to reduce paperwork. It also aims to make payment systems in different countries work together, helping businesses pay suppliers and receive money from customers abroad.
It sets rules for transferring commercial and financial data across borders, limiting requirements for companies to store that information locally, Singapore’s trade ministry said.
Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said exceptions would remain to address concerns over privacy, business confidentiality and national security. Countries would also be able to move at different speeds as they develop their digital systems, he told reporters after the signing.
Putting the agreement into practice
The Asian Development Bank announced on Saturday an initiative aimed at raising up to $5 billion (€4.5bn) in public and private funding by 2030 to support the agreement.
The money would help develop digital infrastructure, payment systems that work across borders and tools to verify identities online, alongside measures to improve cybersecurity.
Gan said differences in countries’ digital readiness had made negotiations difficult. Governments were now identifying projects involving payments, digital identities and electronic trade documents that could be ready when the agreement takes effect.
The deal comes as online business expands across the region. Google, Temasek and Bain & Company forecast that transactions across Southeast Asia’s main digital sectors will reach $368 billion (€333bn) this year and exceed $1 trillion(€905bn) by 2035. Their study covers 10 countries and includes online shopping, travel and food delivery.
“The key measure of success will be what businesses experience on the ground,” said Singapore Business Federation chief executive Kok Ping Soon in a statement released by the trade ministry.

noticias.titulo: Three commercial vessels struck by drones near Romania's black sea, PM says
noticias.resumen: Romania's Prime Minister called the attack on the three vessels Saturday 'unacceptable' and a 'violation of international law'. A day prior, a separate cargo-bound vessel was also struck. No injuries were reported.
noticias.texto:
Romania's Prime Minister called the attack on the three vessels Saturday 'unacceptable' and a 'violation of international law'. A day prior, a separate cargo-bound vessel was also struck. No injuries were reported.
Three commercial vessels were struck on Saturday evening by drones off Romania's Black Sea coast, Romanian authorities confirmed.
The drones struck the vessels near the country's Sulina canal, a key shipping route connecting the Danube river to the Black Sea and used by Ukraine to export goods.
No injuries were reported and the crews managed to extinguish the fires that broke out on board the vessels, Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said.
Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu called the drone attacks "unacceptable" and said it violated international law.
"They reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he wrote on X, pledging to take necessary measures alongside its allies to strengthen security in the Black Sea.
"Romanian Ministry of Defence radars also detected aerial targets in the area," Niculescu said, adding that the Romanian Air Force had sent fighter jets on two separate occasions to investigate.
The ships that were struck included Greek-flagged chemical tanker Evia Petrol V and Saint Kitts and Nevis-flagged bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov.
Earlier on Friday, Ukrainian media reported that another cargo vessel, the Palau-flagged Larissa 1, was hit by a drone while reportedly sailing towards Ukraine.
Russia denied targeting countries neighbouring Ukraine with drones.
Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea is due to meet his counterparts in Brussels next week, where the security situation in the Black Sea is expected to be discussed.
"We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through equipment for counter-drone warfare," Oprea said.

noticias.titulo: Record immigration day in El Hierro as 1,488 arrive in Canary Islands
noticias.resumen: 12 cayucos carrying 1,235 people reached El Hierro on Saturday, and two more boats reached Gran Canaria and Tenerife. The Canaries saw 1,488 arrivals in a day and over 2,300 in two days; President Clavijo said they are overwhelmed.
noticias.texto:
12 cayucos carrying 1,235 people reached El Hierro on Saturday, and two more boats reached Gran Canaria and Tenerife. The Canaries saw 1,488 arrivals in a day and over 2,300 in two days; President Clavijo said they are overwhelmed.
On Saturday, 14 November, 12 large wooden boats arrived in El Hierro carrying 1,235 people. Another 203 people on a boat were intercepted in Gran Canaria. 50 others arrived on a vessel in Tenerife.
The total number, 1,488 people, is a record high for the Canary Islands since 33 small boats and large canoes carrying 1,461 people arrived on 7 November 2020. There were 108 women and 167 minors among yesterday’s arrivals, according to provisional data.
Saturday’s figures do not include two rescue operations still under way or the 122 people travelling in a large canoe that reached La Restinga at 23:55 on Friday. 843 people arrived in 8 boats. The total for the two days is 2,331 people on 22 boats.
A migration system at breaking point
The operation deployed six Maritime Rescue vessels (Diphda, Acrux, Navia, Alpheratz, Mizar and Urania) and two Civil Guard patrol boats (Río Tajo and Río Guadiato).
As of Saturday, there were 317 people at El Hierro’s Temporary Foreigners’ Reception Centre (CATE) , not counting the latest arrivals. 158 people were transferred to Tenerife on the regular ferry service. Eleven people from previous arrivals remain in hospital at Nuestra Señora de los Reyes Island Hospital.
The Canary Islands president, Fernando Clavijo, said that the consistent arrival of boats this month has completely overwhelmed the island’s resources. El Hierro’s island council had already declared a social emergency after the arrival of more than 8,000 people over five weeks.
Clavijo wrote to the European Commissioner for Migration, Magnus Brunner, calling for urgent action in response to the upsurge on the Atlantic route, and announced that Pedro Sánchez had pledged to urgently convene an Interministerial Commission on Immigration. The Minister for Territorial Policy, Ángel Víctor Torres, is due to visit the port of La Restinga on Sunday.
Why are they arriving now and what are people demanding on the island?
The Interior Ministry recorded 6,194 arrivals in October, the month with the greatest migratory pressure on the route since 2023. Forecasts do not point to a decline before December, when weather conditions change along the route of more than 1,000 kilometres linking the Canary Islands with Senegal, Gambia and Mauritania. Canary Islands authorities attribute the surge to a loss of control by the Senegalese security forces, which have been deployed for sporting events in Dakar.
Thimbo Samb, a Senegalese man who has lived in Spain for 20 years, is the central figure in the documentary 'Los cayucos de Kayar', nominated for the Goya Awards.
He links the rise in migration to Ousmane Sonko’s declining influence, saying that President Bassirou Diomaye Faye removed Sonko from government a few months ago. The dismissal intensified the lack of hope caused by corruption and the shortage of work. Samb reached Spain at the age of 17, on his fourth attempt, and argues that safer channels should exist for people to migrate from Africa to Europe.
Txema Santana, a former adviser to the Canary Islands government on migration, believes that the people of El Hierro are not protesting against migrants themselves, but against the authorities’ slow or absent response. He is calling for services to be reinforced without waiting for the high season and for people to be moved off the island as quickly as possible to prevent collapse.

noticias.titulo: Chinese electric passenger plane completes first crewed flight
noticias.resumen: The plane, a CE-25A, took off and landed in Binzhou, Shandong Province, and reportedly flew for around 60 kilometres.
noticias.texto:
The plane, a CE-25A, took off and landed in Binzhou, Shandong Province, and reportedly flew for around 60 kilometres.
A Chinese electric passenger plane completed its first crewed flight on Saturday, marking a historic first for China’s aviation industry and the state-backed Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC), state media reported.
The aircraft was reportedly manned by two pilots and an engineer as it flew for around 60 kilometres, staying airborne for 16 minutes and 38 seconds.
It took off and landed in Binzhou, Shandong Province, in eastern China. China’s state broadcaster CCTV News and the Xinhua news agency first reported on the flight.
The plane, a CE-25A designed for short-distance commercial flights between cities, used an electric propulsion system. It can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 tonnes. It has a cruising speed of up to 300 km per hour and can fly at an altitude of 2,400 metres.
COMAC said the flight "operated normally." The aircraft was built in China as a collaborative effort between COMAC and battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), Shanghai Jiao Tong University and others.
The manned flight is the latest step in the plane's development. It had already flown autonomously in February this year and has since completed 19 unmanned test flights.
The manufacturer applied for type certification from the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) but has yet to receive approval to enter commercial service.

noticias.titulo: Two aircraft collide at Miami International Airport
noticias.resumen: It came as travellers across the US continued to face disruption following a nationwide ground stop that caused chaos at airports this weekend.
noticias.texto:
It came as travellers across the US continued to face disruption following a nationwide ground stop that caused chaos at airports this weekend.
Two aircraft collided at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries, according to officials.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 had struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 as the two planes were taxiing at the southeastern Florida airport.
"Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight," the agency said, adding that the Copa flight was taxiing to the gate and the UPS flight was taxiing for departure to Bogotá.
In a statement to Euronews, MIA communications director Greg Chin said the incident occurred at around 9:15 pm and that there was "no impact to airport operations" as flights were directed to other taxiways.
"Two patients were treated on the scene by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue for minor injuries and did not require medical transport," he added.
Copa Airlines confirmed that one of its planes had been involved in a collision at the airport as it taxied to the terminal after arriving from Panama City.
"According to preliminary information, a collision occurred between a cargo aircraft and the left-wing tip of the Boeing 737-800NG while both aircraft were moving along the airport’s taxiways," the carrier said.
There were 166 passengers and six crew members on board the Copa plane when the incident occurred, it continued, adding that it regretted "any inconvenience and concern this situation may have caused" and that the safety of its passengers and crew members remained its priority.
Images circulating on social media appear to show damage to the nose of the UPS plane.
It came as travellers across the US continued to face disruption following a nationwide ground stop that caused chaos at airports this weekend.
Thousands of flights were cancelled on both Friday and Saturday after the stoppage - which was lifted on Friday evening - was ordered due to a "telecommunications outage."
Airlines are expecting to return to their full operating schedules by Sunday night, the FAA has said.

noticias.titulo: EU forces board suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker in Mediterranean, Kallas says
noticias.resumen: The shadow fleet helps Russia get around Western sanctions on its oil industry by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo.
noticias.texto:
The shadow fleet helps Russia get around Western sanctions on its oil industry by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo.
European Union forces boarded a suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker in the Mediterranean earlier this week, according to Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief.
Troops from the bloc's Operation Irini boarded the MV Midag tanker on Friday and confirmed that the vessel was sailing under a false flag, Kallas said in a post on social media on Sunday.
"The EU will keep disrupting Russia’s shadow fleet at sea and through diplomatic means," she wrote, adding that EU foreign ministers were set to approve new sanctions against Russia on Monday, targeting "banks, buyers and companies supporting the shadow fleet."
Kallas also shared images appearing to show the boarding.
Russia uses its shadow fleet to evade Western sanctions on its oil industry. The shadow fleet gets around these restrictions by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo.
In August, Operation Irini forces carried out a flag verification boarding of the MV Sun oil tanker.
A similar mission also took place earlier in the month targeting the MV Toa Payoh ship.
Operation Irini was launched in March 2020 and was tasked with enforcing an UN arms embargo on Libya due to the Second Libyan Civil War.
Its original mandate was to counter illegal arms trafficking, gather information on oil smuggling, help disrupt human smuggling and train Libyan institutions responsible for law enforcement and search and rescue operations.
In October, Operation Irini's mandate was renewed through to 31 March 2029, with its objectives to include safeguarding the EU's interests in the Mediterranean and continuing to contribute to peace and stability in Libya.
One of its new responsibilities is also to help "constrain" Russia's shadow fleet, which it says uses the Mediterranean as a "key transit and transfer area."

noticias.titulo: Watch: SpaceX catches Starship in midair on return to launch tower
noticias.resumen: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft was successfully caught by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch tower after a 22-hour journey, marking the first successful midair capture of a Starship returning from space.
noticias.texto:
SpaceX's Starship spacecraft was caught in midair by giant mechanical arms at its launch tower in Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, November 14, marking a major milestone for the company's space programme.
The spacecraft returned to Earth after a 22-hour journey, descending upright before being caught by the tower's mechanical arms. Crowds gathered at the site cheered as Starship was secured above the ground.
The successful capture marked the first time a Starship returning from space had been caught by the launch tower. However, SpaceX did not achieve its planned double catch after the first-stage booster exploded shortly after Friday's liftoff.
SpaceX plans to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center in the coming months. The spacecraft is also central to NASA's plans for future Artemis missions to the Moon.

noticias.titulo: Cape Verde heads to the polls in presidential election
noticias.resumen: Incumbent President José Maria Neves, who won the 2021 presidential election, is favoured to win a second term in office.
noticias.texto:
Incumbent President José Maria Neves, who won the 2021 presidential election, is favoured to win a second term in office.
Cape Verdeans are heading to the polls on Sunday to elect the country's next president.
Incumbent President José Maria Neves, favoured to win a second term in office, comes up against five contenders, including Joana Rosa Amado, Cape Verde's first ever female candidate.
Voting starts at 8 am and polls will remain open for 10 hours. Provisional results are expected to come in overnight. If no candidate secures an absolute majority, there will be a second round on 29 November.
Amado, a 61-year-old lawyer backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy (MpD), is running under the slogan "Listen to Cabo Verde," which she says "does not mean promising everything, but rather, knowing the real concerns and expectations of the population."
"The election of a woman to the presidency would show many young women and young girls that no government job is barred from them," she told the media.
The former justice minister has centred her campaign on maintaining a balance of power, arguing that the country needs a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.
For his part, Neves, who won the 2021 presidential election with around 52% of the vote, has pledged to secure cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, as well as to create jobs and raise wages.
Between 2001 and 2016, the 66-year-old served as prime minister and president of the PAICV.
Among the other candidates is surgeon Gilson Alves, 45, an authoritarian figure who promises to fight corruption, allow gun ownership and restore the death penalty.
Cape Verde
Cape Verde sits off the coast of West Africa, around 600 km from Senegal. With roughly half a million inhabitants, it is known for its democratic stability, with a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections.
In July, Cape Verde was officially classified as an upper-middle-income country by the World Bank, due to economic growth in the tourism sector and a 16.8% increase in gross national income per capita between 2023 and 2024.
However, the country faces a number of challenges, including persistent social inequality, geographic isolation and a lack of affordable options for travel between its islands.
Among the main concerns of the local population are the rising cost of living, fuel prices and youth unemployment.

noticias.titulo: SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket in historic first
noticias.resumen: Crowds outside the Texas Starbase erupted into cheers as the mechanical arms closed around the spaceship for the first time, a moment SpaceX said "changed everything."
noticias.texto:
Crowds outside the Texas Starbase erupted into cheers as the mechanical arms closed around the spaceship for the first time, a moment SpaceX said "changed everything."
The upper part of SpaceX's Starship rocket returned to Earth on Saturday, where it was caught between two mechanical "chopstick" arms in what marked the first-ever "catch" of a spaceship.
Starship had lifted off from Starbase in Texas on Friday before orbiting Earth 14 times as it deployed 26 satellites for Elon Musk's Starlink internet constellation.
After a 22-hour journey, the spacecraft approached Texas' east coast, with its three Raptor engines roaring into life as it broke through the clouds and began its descent back to the launchpad.
"Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement!" the company wrote in a post on social media alongside footage of the moment.
"I hugged ship 42 upon its return," SpaceX CEO Musk added in another post on X.
Crowds outside the Starbase erupted into cheers as the mechanical arms closed around the spaceship for the first time, a moment SpaceX said "changed everything."
Spaceships have previously been single-use vehicles, making each launch particularly expensive.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the catch "almost magic."
"Making more believers by the day," he wrote on X. Starship is lined up to serve as a landing system for NASA's Artemis Moon landing mission.
SpaceX had also attempted to guide a Super Heavy rocket booster back to the launch site shortly after Friday's launch. The effort was unsuccessful, however, with the booster "diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf." SpaceX has previously carried out three booster catches.
"The booster’s guidance, navigation and control triggered an automated abort during coast and diverted itself successfully to an offshore landing location," SpaceX said. It added that the boostback burn had "ended early due to low fuel mass" and that the root cause was under investigation.
The successful return of the rocket's upper stage was nevertheless a huge success for Musk and his company.

noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy questions SpaceX over reported Starshield speed restrictions
noticias.resumen: The restrictions have been directly affecting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, Zelenskyy said in an address at the European Political Community summit in Dublin earlier this week.
noticias.texto:
The restrictions have been directly affecting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, Zelenskyy said in an address at the European Political Community summit in Dublin earlier this week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reportedly accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of misleading Kyiv over speed restrictions to its Starshield network.
Zelenskyy said on Thursday that Ukrainian forces were facing restrictions to the service, with terminals limited to a maximum speed of 161 kilometres per hour in areas occupied by Vladimir Putin's invading forces.
"The restrictions have now been in place for five days," the Ukrainian leader said in comments released on Saturday and reported by multiple outlets. "They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case."
The restrictions have been directly affecting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, Zelenskyy said in an address at the European Political Community summit in Dublin earlier this week.
"If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he told the summit.
On Friday, he added that Kyiv had received "no clear explanations" for the curbs.
"I instructed Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Minister of Defense to step up contacts with the U.S. Department of State, the Pentagon, and SpaceX to obtain clarification and resolve the situation," he wrote in a post on social media.
Starshield has proved critical to Ukraine's military operations against Russian forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.
It came as Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to accelerate peace talks continue.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, per the AFP news agency.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.
"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.

noticias.titulo: Judo: double gold for Canada on day 2 at Zagreb Grand Prix
noticias.resumen: Canada celebrated double gold at the Zagreb Grand Prix as Jessica Klimkait and François Gauthier-Drapeau topped the podium. Georgia's Giorgi Loladze and Brazil's Nauana Silva claimed their first Grand Prix titles, while Croatia's Iva Oberan delighted the home crowd with bronze.
noticias.texto:
Canada celebrated double gold at the Zagreb Grand Prix as Jessica Klimkait and François Gauthier-Drapeau topped the podium. Georgia's Giorgi Loladze and Brazil's Nauana Silva claimed their first Grand Prix titles, while Croatia's Iva Oberan delighted the home crowd with bronze.
It's Day 2 of the Zagreb Grand Prix, hosted at the Arena Zagreb, here in the heart of Croatia.
The event was officially opened with a local Kata performance followed by speeches -from Secretary General of the International Judo Federation, Dr Lisa Allan_,_ and President of the Croatian Judo Federation, Dr Sanda Corak.
Day two brought world class judo, putting fans right up close to all the action.
At -63kg, former world champion Jessica KLIMKAIT of Canada was up against Slovenia's Kaja KAJZER ZABKAR. With just seconds to go, a Waza-ari score from KLIMKAIT was enough to take the victory.
Dr Krešimir ŠAMIJA, Croatia Prime Minister Representative, awarded the medals.
Georgia's Giorgi LOLADZE and Joshua GREEN of Ireland were both competing in their first ever Grand Prix final. In a close battle, just a Yuko score would crown LOLADZE the -73Kg champion.
Ambassador of Georgia to Croatia, His Excellency Mr Zaal GOGSADZE awarded the medals.
At -70kg, Nauana SILVA of Brazil met Poland’s Aleksandra KOWALEWSKA in the final. SILVA has 4 Grand Prix medals to her name, but never taken gold. A relentless drive from the Brazilian earned her that elusive first title!
Mr Krešimir MAKVIĆ, City of Zagreb Mayor Representative, awarded the medals.
It was a great day for the Canadian team with François GAUTHIER DRAPEAU at -81Kg providing a fantastic footsweep in golden score, to take Canada’s second gold medal.
The medals were awarded by Ms Tina TRSTENJAK, International Judo Federation Referee Director.
A sensational bronze medal for Croatia’s Iva OBERAN and unstoppable local judo action gave the home crowd plenty to cheer for throughout the day.
We’ll see you tomorrow for the heavyweights on Day 3.

noticias.titulo: Hope springs eternal in award-winning photos showcasing nature’s resilience
noticias.resumen: A fragile Turkish delta and a melting Icelandic 'snow tree' are captured in the award-winning images.
noticias.texto:
Hope springs eternal in award-winning photos showcasing nature’s resilience
A fragile Turkish delta and a melting Icelandic 'snow tree' are captured in the award-winning images.
From wildfire-scorched forests to algae-choked lakes, humans are leaving increasingly indelible marks on nature.
Carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels are pushing global warming towards and beyond the 1.5°C limit, resulting in ever worsening weather extremes.
Mass consumption is strewing coastlines with waste and polluting waterways with chemicals.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, and the European Environment Agency’s (EEA) latest state of the environment report found more than 80 per cent of protected habitats in poor or bad condition.
With the UN’s COP31 summit now in full swing, world leaders are coming together to get climate action back on track. Hot on the heels of the COP17 biodiversity talks, which ended on 31 October with a new roadmap but a UN report showing the world is falling behind on its 2030 nature goals, the intersection between nature and climate has been thrown into the spotlight.
It’s a relationship Europeans were invited to explore for this year’s EEA ‘Resilient by Nature’ photo competition.
Photographers from 35 countries set out to capture nature in states of harmony, disruption or renewal. From almost 2,800 entries, an external jury chose a winner in each category, as well as awarding a youth prize. The images were also put to a public online vote for the public choice award.
Harmony: Humans and nature find balance in Türkiye’s ancient delta
Türkiye’s Dalyan Delta has for decades stood strong against tourism development, with strict environmental protections helping to fight off resorts and other human activity.
Designated as a Special Environmental Protection Area in the 1980s, the ecologically vital wetland ecosystem is home to over 150 bird species and rare, endemic Turkish sweetgum forests.
Vulnerable loggerhead sea turtles nest on İztuzu Beach, where seasonal night closures and a ban on pets are in place to protect hatchlings.
Still, humans have long made their mark there: Lycian rock-cut tombs are carved into the cliffs along the delta’s labyrinthine channels, while the ruins of the ancient port city of Kaunos hark back to an era of maritime trading.
Now, eco-tourism, local fishing and wildlife preservation bring a slower pace to the delta – the delicate balance of which was captured from above by award-winning photographer Ali Aslan.
Disruption: A water rail wades through a rubbish-lined drainage pipe
Reminding us of what happens when humans neglect their duties of protection, Spanish photographer Julián Fernandez Quilez placed a remote-triggered, wide-angle setup inside a drainage pipe.
He captured a secretive wetland water rail wading through the murky, rubbish-filled pipe, probing a disposable medical face mask, bottle caps and a crushed drink can with its long red bill.
In the background, a watery habitat can be spied through the drain’s opening, putting into focus the consequences of human encroachment on natural ecosystems.
Renewal: A green shoot springs from a scorched landscape
Extreme heat and prolonged drought made 2026 among the worst years on record for wildfires, with nearly 700,000 hectares burned by August, according to the European Commission – nearly double the 20-year historical average.
The impacts are far-reaching: destroyed ecosystems and farmland, degraded soil, planet-heating emissions, health-harming air and water pollution that knows no borders.
While many of these landscapes will take decades to heal – and some will be changed irrevocably – Sofia-based photographer Elitsa Mihaylova reminds us of nature’s remarkable ability to heal.
Her image of a green shoot rising from the ashes appears “fragile, almost impossible, yet full of quiet strength”, according to the photo’s caption.
Youth Prize: Scat research and camera traps rewarded with rare sighting
Eighteen-year-old wildlife photographer Denat Lahi spends weeks mapping territories, photographing scat, and cross-referencing local wildlife databases in his home city of Lund, Sweden.
Lahi uses this intel to identify the best locations for capturing human-like emotion in mammals, he told photography news site PetaPixel.
His dedication has paid off: an image from his series following elusive pine martens in Sweden was awarded the Youth Prize by EEA.
Using nighttime camera trapping and motion-sensing, he snapped the curious creature exploring a dilapidated barn filled with industrial materials – a rare insight into the shy animals’ nocturnal forays into human environments.
Public Choice Award: Melting snow draws a ‘tree of life’ across Iceland’s highlands
Melting snow carves delicate lines in the Icelandic Highlands, with glowing green moss spreading like roots and branches. Barely perceptible from the ground, the scale and natural symmetry of the phenomenon is captured spectacularly by aerial landscape photographer Radoslav Sviretsov.
While snow in this northern wilderness naturally fades between May and June, warmer spring temperatures spurred by climate change are causing it to vanish earlier and earlier, while mild winters are hindering its ability to rebuild and disrupting water cycles.
Open to all European citizens and EEA member countries above 18 years old, the EEA photo competition is free to enter. It aims to bring light to the beauty of Europe’s nature, the environmental challenges it grapples with, and the solutions close at hand.

noticias.titulo: Feeling the winter chill? Thermal baths and scenic outdoor saunas worth visiting in Europe
noticias.resumen: Whether it’s floating saunas in Norway or steaming thermal baths in Budapest, Europe offers travellers some spectacular spots to take on the winter chill.
noticias.texto:
Whether it’s floating saunas in Norway or steaming thermal baths in Budapest, Europe offers travellers some spectacular spots to take on the winter chill.
Instead of retreating indoors to escape the winter chill, why not embrace it? Across Europe, thermal baths and outdoor saunas offer the perfect opportunity for wellness and to warm up.
Centuries-old bathing traditions and complexes remain a popular way to unwind across the continent.
So, if you’re looking to enjoy Europe's colder months in a different way, here are some warming places worth adding to your winter travel bucket list.
Thermal baths
Bathing beneath the aurora, Iceland
For Northern Lights chasers, Iceland’s Laugarás Lagoon combines geothermal bathing with the spectacular sights of the natural phenomenon.
The two-level lagoon on the banks of the Hvítá river is open well into the evening during winter and sits just over an hour's drive from Reykjavík. Visitors can enjoy aurora viewing at the backdrop of darker skies, when conditions allow.
The geothermal waters hover between temperatures of 37C and 39C, and, for a true Icelandic experience afterwards, visitors can brave the cold with a plunge in the pool, which is fed fresh river water.
Széchenyi Thermal Bath in Budapest, Hungary
Hungary’s capital Budapest is home to Széchenyi Thermal Bath, which is one of the largest spa complexes on the continent.
Its thermal section comprises three indoor pools, with the thermal water pool’s temperature ranging from 28C to 40C. Meanwhile, the outdoor thermal pool’s temperature is anywhere from 36C to 38C.
The water supply comes from the Saint Stephen Well Nr. II, which is made up of calcium, magnesium, and sodium, among other minerals. The mineral-rich waters are thought to be beneficial for supporting degenerative joint diseases as well as chronic and subacute arthritis.
Emser Therme in Bad Ems, Germany
Emser Therme offers an array of indoor and outdoor pools with temperatures between 18C and 38C. The indoor thermal pool hovers at 33C and features a small seating area with bubble jets. There is also a hot bubble pool and warmer indoor thermal pool at 36C.
At its Sidroga herbal steam bath, visitors are recommended to stay for no more than 15 minutes in the high humidity experience. It is set at 47C and has scents of camomile, sage, peppermint and thyme.
Its thermal water contains more than 30 minerals and trace elements. Emser Therme recommends no longer than a 20-minute stay in thermal water, accompanied by 20 to 30 minutes’ rest afterwards.
Bains Romains de Dorres in the French Pyrenees
At an altitude of 1,450 metres in the French Pyrenees, and offering sweeping views of the valleys, Bains Romains de Dorres has two outdoor pools where visitors can soak in waters heated to between 37C and 40C.
For those with muscle aches or pains, it recommends an hour’s soak in the baths for a soothing effect.
Thermae Bath Spa in Bath, England
One of the city’s most popular attractions, Thermae Bath Spa has four baths on offer at 35.3C, including an open-air rooftop pool with views of the skyline.
This spa is also home to the UK’s only day spa that features Bath’s natural thermal waters made of 42 minerals and trace elements – which were once enjoyed by the Celts and Romans more than 2,000 years ago.
Scenic outdoor saunas
Lakeside sauna at Alpenhotel Kitzbühel in Kitzbühel, Austria
For a view of Austria's Lake Schwarzsee while you unwind, check into Alpenhotel Kitzbühel and make a beeline for its lakeside sauna.
Located outside the hotel’s wellness area, the sauna is open year-round and temperatures can reach up to 90C.
Beyond the lake, visitors can also see the Wilder Kaiser mountain range and the Kitzbühel mountains.
Floating saunas in Aurland and Flåm, Norway
On the Aurlandsfjord in Norway, a sauna sits atop a floating dock surrounded by mountain views. Open three times a week during the winter season, FjordSauna offers a space that can accommodate up to 12 people. Visitors can book shared or private experiences, with a guided ritual available for the latter.
Sessions are no longer than one and a half hours, and alternate between steamy and cold fjord plunges.
In Flåm, evening "aufguss" rituals are a winter speciality. This is where a sauna master pours water mixed with essential oils onto the hot sauna stones alongside curated music. The guided session lasts 60 minutes for groups of up to eight people.
Archipelago sauna at Skärgårdens Kanotcenter, Sweden
In Resarö, Sweden, the crackle of firewood and hiss of steam comes with a sea view. The Skärgårdens Kanotcenter offers visitors one-and-a-half-hour sessions, where the sauna temperature ranges between 60C and 80C. Wood is provided on-site, for visitors to tend to the fire as they please.
